High-Delta-theta sites preferentially exhibit larger thermal nonaffine motion and stronger thermal deviatoric strain, particularly in the deeply jammed regime, indicating that geometrically frustrated regions are preferentially associated with localized mechanical distortions. The thermal volumetric response exhibits a distinct mismatch-dependent crossover: low-Delta-theta sites predominantly contribute to the small-strain response, whereas high-Delta-theta sites contribute more strongly to the large-strain tail. The contrast between low- and high-mismatch populations is most pronounced in the deeply jammed regime, remains identifiable through the intermediate viscoelastic regime, and progressively weakens upon heating toward the liquid state. These results establish a direct connection between local steric frustration and thermally activated mechanical response, showing that thermal nonaffine metrics and thermal strain fields provide a physically transparent bridge between local structure and thermally driven rearrangements in amorphous glasses.
2611.11939.comment: Submitted to Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications
2611.11939.title: Topology to Elasticity Mapping in Thermal Glass

2611.11953.abstract: Most turbulent flows are sustained by inertia, which transfers energy across scales and produces characteristic power-law spectra. Yet dilute polymer solutions also exhibit turbulence when inertia is negligible: in this state, known as elastic turbulence, the velocity field remains spatially smooth while both the velocity and the polymer conformation exhibit robust power-law spectra. How a smooth flow, lacking a hierarchy of eddies, generates such multiscale structure has remained unexplained. Here we show that the missing mechanism is elastic frontogenesis, whereby the flow spontaneously organizes polymer stress into thin sheets that are stretched within their plane and compressed across their thickness, causing their amplitude to grow as they become thinner. Because the fronts are sheet-like structures, this amplification-thinning law uniquely determines the polymer conformation spectrum, while the Stokes response transfers the same geometric scaling to the velocity field, reconciling broadband spectra with spatial smoothness. Being geometric rather than model-specific, elastic frontogenesis provides an organizing principle for viscoelastic flows and the viscoelastic analogue of vortex stretching in inertial turbulence.
2611.11953.title: Elastic frontogenesis sets the spectra of smooth elastic turbulence

2611.11958.abstract: Biomolecular recognition and regulation depend on atomic interactions that change as molecular partners fluctuate and adopt alternative conformations. Modeling these processes requires ensembles that capture both conformational diversity and coordinated atomic fluctuations between interacting molecules. Here we present OriDynamics, a unified framework for all-atom ensemble generation across protein monomers and complexes with small molecules or protein partners. OriDynamics introduces a latent ensemble decomposition that couples broad conformational exploration in a compact structural latent space with local all-atom sampling around generated proposals. Ensemble-level supervision constrains mean positions, fluctuation amplitudes and joint coordinate covariance to capture coordinated atomic variability within and between molecular partners. Across benchmarks of proteins and their complexes, OriDynamics demonstrates superior overall performance in conformational coverage, atomic fluctuation fidelity and interaction geometry compared with leading baselines. Application studies further demonstrate recovery of alternative functional conformations and partner-dependent changes in conformational ensembles alongside sampling of configurations associated with ligand dissociation. These capabilities provide a foundation for a biomolecular world model that represents accessible molecular states and their dependence on interaction context.
2611.11958.comment: 29 pages, 6 main figures and 5 supplementary figures. Includes supplementary information
2611.11958.title: OriDynamics: Towards a World Model for Biomolecular Dynamics

2611.12298.abstract: Instability phenomena are ubiquitous in multi-fluid flows. For binary fluid mixtures, phase separation may occur under specific conditions, in which a homogeneous state becomes unstable and spontaneously segregates into different phases, leading to the formation of distinct patterns. Furthermore, when a heavier fluid is superposed over a lighter one in a gravitational field, the fluid interface can be sensitive to perturbations that trigger the Rayleigh--Taylor (RT) instability, i.e., the lighter fluid penetrates upward into the heavier fluid against gravity. We investigate such instability phenomena and the inhibiting conditions for incompressible, immiscible two-phase flows with unmatched densities, within the framework of a diffuse-interface model, which is called the Abels--Garcke--Grün (AGG) model. More precisely, we adopt energy methods to establish several stability/instability conditions for the perturbed system of the AGG model, which is obtained by slightly perturbing the equilibrium profile $(\mathbf{0},\overline{\varphi})$, where $\overline{\varphi}=\overline{\varphi}(x_3)$ depends solely on the vertical coordinate $x_3$. Notably, for a constant equilibrium profile $\overline{\varphi}=α\in(-1,1)$ satisfying $Ψ''(α)<0$, we establish a threshold for stability and instability of the phase-separation problem.Similar stability results are also established for the perturbed system with $\overline{\varphi}$ satisfying the RT instability condition in the presence of gravity. In particular, if the phase-separation condition fails and $\partial_{x_3}\overline{\varphi}$ is a constant, a larger value of $\partial_{x_3}\overline{\varphi}$, a greater interfacial thickness and a higher surface energy density contribute to inhibiting RT instability.
2611.12298.title: On the Abels--Garcke--Grün Model for Incompressible Two-Phase Flows with Unmatched Densities: Phase Separation and Rayleigh--Taylor Instability

2611.12322.abstract: Y6-based homojunction organic photovoltaic devices have recently achieved exceptional power conversion efficiencies, surpassing those of conventional organic photovoltaic materials. Although unusually long exciton diffusion lengths and efficient exciton dissociation have been reported, the fundamental mechanism underlying this outstanding performance remains under debate. Here, we report that structurally distinct aggregates in Y6 thin films exhibit complementary charge-transfer (CT) characters that enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. Using ultrafast spectroscopy, we identify highly efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between Y6 aggregates, with an ensemble-averaged efficiency of 65% occurring on a sub-picosecond timescale (<1 ps). This aggregate-mediated energy-transfer pathway drives long-range energy migration in Y6 thin films and accounts for the remarkable external quantum efficiencies observed in homojunction devices, even in the absence of conventional donor-acceptor bulk heterojunction morphologies and despite substantial fractions of weak-CT components. Here, using Y6 as a model non-fullerene acceptor (NFA) system, we show that structurally distinct aggregates coexisting in NFA thin films possess complementary CT characters, which are expected to enable directional energy transfer and enhanced exciton delocalization. We establish a general multi-component FRET framework that quantitatively links molecular aggregation, CT character, and excited-state dynamics in systems with multiple packing motifs. This work provides insight into the development of next-generation high-performance organic electronic materials and devices.
2611.12322.title: Ultrafast Inter-Aggregate Energy Transfer Drives Efficient Charge Generation in Organic Homojunctions

2611.12578.abstract: We present a class of numerical collocation methods to solve a typical inverse problem that arises in the stress-controlled rheology of complex fluids with pronounced history-dependent response, where the relation between stress and flow rate is given by an integral constitutive equation as the material law. We demonstrate the method by calculating the creep response of a nontrivial model of a shear-thinning viscoelastic fluid where a stress overshoot in rate-controlled startup flow leads to ``sudden yielding'' in stress-controlled creep. Our method is able to address the long-time behavior of the model, distinguishing the amorphous solid from the stress-induced yielded fluid, and from the in-between case of infinite deformation that never achieves a stationary shear rate (proper creep). To this end, we implement a method with flexible time-stepping, and prove uniqueness of the solution and convergence of the methods for a broad class of highly viscoelastic non-linear rheological laws in integral form.
2611.12578.comment: 45 pages, 5 figures, for an implementation that also has been used to create the figures see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22978793
2611.12578.title: Nonlinear integral equations for stress-controlled rheology: Collocation methods for Volterra equations with functional kernels

2611.12735.abstract: Catalysis can drive phase separation by coupling local chemical composition to molecular transport, even in the absence of attractive interactions. Here, we demonstrate such catalysis-induced phase separation in a microscopic particle-based model of enzymes catalyzing the interconversion of substrate and product molecules with different diffusivities. We derive an analytical instability criterion in the dilute limit, showing that a homogeneous mixture becomes unstable when the nonequilibrium chemical drive and the diffusivity contrast are sufficiently large, and the substrate and product concentration exceeds a threshold set by the enzyme volume. Brownian-dynamics simulations confirm the predicted instability and reveal macroscopic coexistence of enzyme-rich and enzyme-poor phases, including in regimes where equilibrium depletion interactions cannot account for demixing. Finally, we show that, upon eliminating the fast chemical degrees of freedom, the reactive ternary mixture maps onto an effective binary mixture nonreciprocal interactions. Our results establish an explicit microscopic mechanism for catalysis-induced phase separation and connect chemically driven phase separation to the physics of motility-regulated and nonreciprocal matter.
2611.12735.title: Catalysis-induced phase separation of enzymes via diffusivity contrast

2611.13088.abstract: A central question in holography is how different boundary observables encode and reconstruct the geometry of the gravitational dual. In this work, we uncover an exact geometric correspondence between two seemingly distinct aspects of strongly coupled dynamics: the dissipative drag force experienced by a moving heavy particle(quark) and the entanglement membrane governing the propagation of quantum information. We show that both constructions retain the same underlying structure of the geometry, leading to an invertible transformation between the finite-velocity drag force and the geometric membrane tension. This correspondence reveals that nonlinear momentum loss encodes detailed information about entanglement dynamics: the leading nonlinear correction determines the butterfly velocity, while higher-order terms successively probe the local geometry of the membrane near the horizon. We further connect this hierarchy to scalar pole-skipping, establishing an all-order relation between nonlinear dissipation and near-horizon spectral data. The shared geometric structure also has implications for quantum information recovery, with the quintic drag coefficient determining the leading dependence of information velocity on initial entanglement. Conversely, the complete information-velocity curve provides a reconstruction of the reduced bulk geometry along the physical interior membrane branch, complementing the exterior reconstruction from drag. We show that stochastic momentum broadening supplies the additional radial information needed to reconstruct the complete exterior metric up to an overall scale. Our results thus reveal how dissipation, entanglement dynamics, and spectral properties provide complementary access to holographic geometry, establishing a unified framework for understanding the geometric information encoded in distinct boundary observables.
2611.13088.comment: 64 pages, comments and references are welcome;
2611.13088.title: Holographic Drag Force and the Entanglement Membrane: Geometric Reconstruction and Information Spreading

2611.13101.abstract: Quantum-chaotic systems share the same coarse-grained features characteristic of random matrices, such as Wigner-Dyson level-spacing statistics, yet can exhibit strikingly different eigenstate structure and many-body dynamics, including relaxation, transport, scrambling, and entanglement growth. This raises the fundamental question of whether these finer-grained features probe genuinely distinct aspects of quantum chaos or, instead, reflect different manifestations of a common underlying structure---and whether such structure provides a meaningful basis for regarding one many-body quantum system as "more chaotic" than another. Here, we address this question by introducing a quantum geometric framework that quantifies the susceptibility of many-body eigenstates to physically allowed deformations of the Hamiltonian, as constrained by spatial locality, symmetries, and conservation laws. The resulting geometric susceptibility is quantitative, providing a metric of chaos beyond traditional binary diagnostics; intrinsic, as it depends on the manifold of allowed Hamiltonian deformations rather than on the way the system is probed; and unifying, as it directly connects eigenstate structure with dynamics. For canonical models of quantum chaos, we find that minimal geometric susceptibility, maximal eigenstate randomness, broad spectral response of local operators, and the suppression of nonhydrodynamic slow structure coalesce in the same region of Hamiltonian control space. This suggests that these seemingly distinct signatures of chaos are different manifestations of a common underlying geometric structure. Our framework provides a route toward understanding the limits of relaxation and scrambling under physical constraints; in applications, it offers a means to engineer strongly chaotic regimes in programmable quantum systems with restricted controls.
2611.13101.comment: 18 pages, 9 figures; main text 14 pages, 7 figures
2611.13101.title: Quantum Control Geometry as a Metric of Chaos

2611.13110.abstract: Coarse-grained measurements provide a lower bound on entropy production, but how much microscopic irreversibility can they conceal? We construct a driven quantum system in which an imperfect counter registers a finite, strictly positive arrow of time while the microscopic entropy production is infinite. The system is a degenerate parametric oscillator below threshold, coupled to a thermal reservoir through repeated interactions with bosonic ancillas. The oscillator sustains a finite, positive heat current into the vacuum bath, where absorption is forbidden and forward and reverse trajectory laws have different supports. A photon counter with finite collection efficiency, gated time bins, and independent dark counts defines a common coarse-graining of the aligned trajectory laws. For fixed observation duration $\mathcal T$ and detector parameters, we prove that the observed relative entropy remains uniformly bounded as the bath temperature $T_b$ vanishes and is strictly positive at vacuum. The hidden contribution obeys $Σ_{\mathrm{hid}}(\mathcal T,T_b)=\mathcal T\dot Q_0/(k_BT_b)+O(1)$, where $\dot Q_0>0$ is the stationary vacuum heat current. False positives conceal the support mismatch while preserving measurable time asymmetry. Thus, finite and informative measurements of entropy production can coexist with infinite microscopic irreversibility.
2611.13110.title: Finite Measured Entropy Production Does Not Imply Finite Microscopic Irreversibility

2611.13536.abstract: Catalysis underpins chemical manufacturing, yet knowledge for catalyst design remains dispersed across experimental observations, computational data and catalysis subdisciplines. To overcome this challenge, we present Composable Catalytic Intelligence (CatAI), a physics-grounded modular AI framework that learns 1.8 million structure-property relations and organizes them into 30 physicochemical encoders. This reusable intermediate layer enables task-specific models to guide catalyst discovery for targeted reactions and objectives. Across benchmark tasks, CatAI achieves a 7.8% lower task-averaged prediction error than the next-best models. In experimental validation, CatAI identified a new confined-passable pocket catalyst applicable in industrial homogeneous polymer synthesis with 9 times the activity of the commercial benchmark. In parallel, it guided autonomous closed-loop optimization of a highly active Cu-based geminal-atom photocatalyst for C-O coupling reactions surpassing the traditional Ni-based systems. This approach connects property-level data to catalytic objectives, supporting physicochemical knowledge reuse across mechanistically distinct systems through computational screening and iterative model-experiment feedback.
2611.13536.title: Adaptive catalyst discovery emerges from composable scientific intelligence

2611.13622.abstract: We study the stochastic dynamics of a system of $N$ polymer rings on an infinite cylinder with only excluded volume interaction, using simulations and also analytically. The strings can diffuse in the transverse direction by local Rouse-like moves where an up-kink changes to a down -kink, or vice versa. The motion is biased if the rates of flip are not equal. In the initial state, we start with a step initial condition: all the sites with a positive $y$ coordinate are empty, and the sites with $y \leq 0$ are occupied with a uniform density. We study the scaling form of the density profile in the hydrodynamic limit. The scaling form is a function of $y/\sqrt{t}$ in the unbiased case, and a function of $y/t$ in the biased case. In the unbiased case, in the steady state on a torus, the marginal probability distribution of the positions of the strings on a line with fixed $x$-coordinate is exactly same as that in the ground state of quantum-mechanical spin-less fermions on a line. The biased problem is equivalent to a growing surface in $2+1$ dimension, which is expected to be in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class.
2611.13622.title: Stochastic evolution of interacting directed strings

2611.13800.abstract: Transferring atomic quantum sensors from laboratory-scale physics packages to compact, alignment-free sensor heads suitable for field and space deployment requires a structural platform that combines mechanical, thermal, and optical functionality within a single, manufacturable component. We present such a platform based on additively manufactured technical ceramics: lithography-based ceramic manufacturing is used to fabricate monolithic micro-optical benches with application-specific mounting geometries, while high-precision active alignment and adhesive bonding realize long-term stable optical assemblies through micro-integration. As a first system-level demonstrator, we present a micro-integrated optical frequency reference based on Doppler-free spectroscopy of the rubidium D2 line, integrated within a 6 mL Al2O3 module. A laser stabilized to the reference reaches a fractional frequency instability of $3\times10^{-12}$ at 1 s. We extend the platform to a compact optically pumped magnetometer, exploiting the magnetic cleanliness and tailored thermal properties of high-purity ceramics for a 7 mL sensor head with picotesla sensitivity aimed at space-borne biomagnetometry, and to a micro-integrated optical dipole trap with active MEMS-mirror beam steering for cold-atom manipulation. Together, these demonstrators show that ceramic additive manufacturing and optical micro-integration form a versatile, robust platform for compact atomic sensor systems in field and space applications.
2611.13800.comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Presented at the International Conference on Space Optics (ICSO) 2026; to be published in the ICSO 2026 Proceedings, SPIE Digital Library
2611.13800.title: Additively manufactured ceramic platforms for miniaturized optical frequency references and robust atomic sensor systems

2611.13969.abstract: The design and control of rheological properties in active systems are crucial for developing functional materials with novel properties. While significant attention has been devoted to odd viscosity and odd elasticity, comprehensive odd rheological models remain scarce. Here, we introduce and characterise a platform-agnostic odd viscoelastic material, where complex responses arise from parametric control of internal rotational degrees of freedom and are triggered by coupling between normal and shear stresses. Such control can be achieved through either parametric driving or a parametric nonlinear feedback. We further show that this coupling can induce rotation-driven fluidisation, transitioning the material from an elasticity-dominated to a viscosity-dominated regime. Lastly, we show that the interplay between odd and even sectors enhances the nonlinear material response under large-amplitude oscillatory shear (LAOS). The findings outline a route to Floquet-engineered metafluids with programmable, non-reciprocal rheology.
2611.13969.title: Rheology of Parametric Odd Materials

2611.13983.abstract: Robotic additive manufacturing requires joint paths that reconcile robot feasibility with process-specific geometry. We develop an offline optimization-based path planner that combines joint-path regularity and self-collision penalties with process costs and constraints, so that a new process enters through its own reference, residuals, and tolerances. Full-path and boundary-coupled chunked optimization handle references of different lengths. Iterative Weight Tuning (IWT) determines the cost weights from the gaps between Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and their targets. In carbon-fiber winding and robotic 3D printing, the planned paths meet the geometric tolerances and all KPI targets, and both paths are executed on a UR10e, without extrusion for printing, with joint-level tracking recorded during execution.
2611.13983.comment: Submitted for the review in ECC 2027
2611.13983.title: Optimization-Based Path Planning for Industrial Manipulators: Experimental Validation in Additive Manufacturing

2611.14039.abstract: We introduce the word thermalization hypothesis according to which in a literary work there are effective interactions between words that drive them to thermalization where their word frequency distribution is the same as for the phenomenon of Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation. In this concept, the different words play a role of classical oscillators (particles) and their word frequencies, or related tokens, are analogous to certain filling factors over energy state levels. The thermalization process is characterized by the conservation of total system energy, or total number of words/tokens, and total probability norm, or total number of different words. We apply this approach to analyze 16 literary works, including Bible, complete works of Shakespeare, and data from American National Corpus. We show that for these cases the effective system energy is very low and thus there is the RJ condensation phenomenon with a big fraction of total probability concentrated at the lowest energy states corresponding to a big fraction of rare words appearing only once or twice in the whole text. Such a RJ condensation is observed for light propagation in multimode optical fibers and other physical systems. We relate the thermalization of words to the recently proposed wealth thermalization for households in world countries. The economy concepts of Lorenz and Pareto curves, and also Zipf curves, are applied to the word frequency distributions of the selected 16 cases and it is shown that the thermalization theory gives a strikingly good description of real data.
2611.14039.comment: 30 pages, 6 main figures, 14 appendix figures, journal style file and bbl file for references provided
2611.14039.title: Thermodynamics of words

2611.14104.abstract: Recent work identified spatially localised midplane stress structures as the building blocks of chaotic behaviour in pressure-driven parallel shear flows of viscoelastic fluids. Such coherent structures are thought to originate from a linear centre-mode instability of the laminar state. In the absence of inertia, however, the Oldroyd-B and FENE-P constitutive models predict that this instability is confined to ultra-dilute polymer solutions and very large Weissenberg numbers in channel flow, while no purely elastic instability has been reported in pipe flow. Here, we study numerically the linear stability of channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner (sPTT) fluid and find a purely elastic centre-mode instability in both geometries across a wide range of polymer concentrations and at much lower Weissenberg numbers. Since the sPTT and FENE-P models have identical steady rheology and laminar profiles, their contrasting predictions indicate that the existence of the centre-mode instability is governed by the transient rheological response of the fluid. Our results suggest that the purely elastic centre-mode instability should be observable under realistic flow conditions. They also offer a means of discriminating between constitutive models.
2611.14104.title: Purely elastic centre-mode instability in channel and pipe flows of a simplified Phan-Thien-Tanner fluid

2611.14165.abstract: Understanding thermal transport in structurally disordered carbon materials remains a fundamental challenge because conventional models based on a single coherence contribution cannot accurately describe heat conduction over a broad temperature range. In this work, the thermal conductivity of graphene oxide (GO), thermally reduced graphene oxide (trGO), GO-hydrated fullerene composites (GO-HyFn), expanded graphite (EG), and EG-multiwalled carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composites was measured between 4.5 and 300 K. Despite substantial differences in density, porosity, graphitic ordering, and microstructure, all materials exhibit glass-like temperature dependence of thermal conductivity.   The experimental results demonstrate that the conventional two-channel model, comprising a Peierls contribution and a single thermally activated coherence term, systematically fails to reproduce the observed temperature dependence. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a generalized multichannel phenomenological model in which the coherence contribution consists of up to three Arrhenius-type channels with distinct activation energies. Depending on the structural state, two or three coherence channels are required to accurately describe the thermal conductivity.   A key finding is the reproducible hierarchy of activation energies across diverse carbon allotropes, following approximately (E2 ~ 4E1 and E3 ~ (12-25)E1). While the channel amplitudes increase with material density, the activation energies remain nearly invariant, indicating universal vibrational energy scales. The proposed framework also consistently describes published data for other disordered carbon materials. These results provide experimental evidence for multichannel coherence-mediated heat transport and establish a unified phenomenological bridge between structural hierarchy with thermal transport in disordered carbon solids.
2611.14165.comment: 29 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables; experimental and theoretical analysis of thermal transport in carbon allotropes
2611.14165.title: Universal Multichannel Coherence-Mediated Thermal Transport in Carbon Allotropes: Experimental Evidence and Scaling Laws

2611.14167.abstract: For $K\ge4$ let $E_K(N)$ be the number of integers $2\le n\le N$ for which $K/n=1/x+1/y+1/z$ has no solution in positive integers; $K=4$ is the Erdős-Straus equation. We prove that $E_K(N)\le N\exp(-c((\log N)^3/K)^{1/4})$ with absolute constants $c,B>0$, uniformly for $4\le K\le(\log N)^3/B$. This improves the exponent $2/3$ of Vaughan's bound of 1970. The bound is non-trivial for $K$ up to a constant times $(\log N)^3$, which is, up to a factor $(\log\log N)^{2+o(1)}$, the scale at which, by work of Pomerance and Weingartner, exceptional primes become common. The sieve is combinatorial: a truncated inclusion-exclusion over the classes of parametric solutions, whose second moment is the partition function of a two-copy polymer gas, bounded by a real form of the Kotecký-Preiss criterion. Averaging over the residue classes of the small primes gives the family its full mass, and summing each cluster in a random order bounds the cluster sums. Since a divisor of an exception is an exception, nothing about the small primes themselves is needed, and the sieve can use the classes of the whole family of parametric solutions, one triple per class. All constants are explicit, and the whole proof has been checked in the proof assistant Lean 4.
2611.14167.title: The exponent $3/4$ for the exceptional sets of the equations $K/n=1/x+1/y+1/z$

2611.14341.abstract: This paper studies the numerical approximation of a mathematical model of coupled flow and viscoelastic deformation in a fractured porous medium including fracture contact mechanics. We consider a mixed-dimensional model, where the fracture is modeled as a co-dimension one object within the porous medium. This model couples Darcy flow in the matrix and fracture, linear viscoelasticity of the matrix and frictional contact mechanics of the fracture surfaces; the contact conditions include normal compliance and a Coulomb friction law. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution is established, and stability and a priori error estimates are derived. A numerical experiment is performed in which numerical error estimates are computed and compared to the theoretical results.
2611.14341.title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium

2611.14565.abstract: We introduce a hands-on experimental method that enables students to fabricate and operate van der Waals semiconductor-based field-effect transistors (FETs) using readily available materials and minimal infrastructure. The approach is based on ionic-gel gating using commercially available hydrogel conductors originally developed for muscle electrostimulation devices. For device fabrication we rely on commercially available thin-film interdigitated electrode arrays and for the semiconductor channel, we deposited MoS2 flakes produced by high-throughput mechanical exfoliation. By avoiding the need for cleanroom processing, vacuum deposition, or custom electrolytes, this method allows functional FETs based on van der Waals materials to be realized in a standard teaching laboratory. The experiment is well suited for undergraduate and early graduate courses and is intended to complement concepts introduced in electronics and solid-state physics by providing students with first-hand experience in the fabrication and electrical characterization of emerging electronic devices. Representative electrical measurements demonstrate gate-dependent modulation of the channel conductance and illustrate characteristic features of ionic-gated transistor operation. Overall, the proposed platform provides an accessible route for students to fabricate, characterize, and analyze field-effect devices without access to conventional semiconductor foundry.
2611.14565.title: Hands-on fabrication of 2D material field-effect transistors for the classroom using off-the-shelf ionic gel

2611.14720.abstract: Manipulating polymer chains by means of experimental instruments such as optical tweezers has helped understand better the effects of molecular forces in macromolecular structures. In this study, we simulate the influence of a pulling force on structural phases of a coarse-grained model for flexible polymers using generalized-ensemble Monte Carlo methodologies. The recently introduced microcanonical inflection-point analysis method is employed to identify and classify structural phases of the system. Specific order parameters help characterize the transition behavior in response to the present pulling force. We show that, upon increasing the pulling strength, the coil-globule transition turns from second to first order, then merges with the liquid-solid transition. An intermediate phase, separating the coil and globule phases, is identified for certain force strengths. Clear evidence of the Gough-Joule effect is found as well. Transitions do not occur at all if the pulling force exceeds a certain threshold value.
2611.14720.title: Force-Dependent Change of Structural Behavior Upon Pulling a Grafted Flexible Polymer

2611.14872.abstract: The rheometry of soft, tissue-like materials at ultra-high strain rates is critical to biomechanics, materials science, and medical engineering. One approach for characterizing high-rate material response is Inertial Microcavitation Rheometry (IMR), which infers viscoelastic constitutive behavior from the measured radius-time history of a laser-induced cavitation bubble. At these rates, materials may exhibit history-dependent behavior, including damage, fracture, and plasticity. However, conventional IMR analyses typically assume constant material properties throughout the cavitation event, limiting their ability to capture such changes. We present an IMR framework for identifying effective time varying material properties from measured cavitation radius histories. The framework allows the shear modulus, viscosity, or both to evolve during the event using normalized sigmoid histories. Synthetic tests recover prescribed constant and time varying material histories. Application to polyacrylamide and gelatin datasets yields effective material-property histories across formulations and experimental conditions. Viscosity decreased across the datasets, while the extent of shear modulus reduction varied with material and formulation. When both properties decreased, their reductions could occur at different stages of cavitation. This distinction in mechanical property degradation depends on both the property and its evolution during high-strain events.
2611.14872.title: Soft material mechanical property degradation at high strain rates

2611.15656.abstract: Advances in 3D nanophotonic additive manufacturing enable increasingly complex, almost free-form devices for manipulating light at sub-wavelength scales. Extending nanophotonic designs into three dimensions introduces additional degrees of freedom. Exploiting this freedom requires inverse-design methods that can efficiently navigate this large design space while accommodating fabrication constraints. Here, we combine gradient-free optimization with the level-set method (LSM) to provide such an approach for 3D additive manufacturing. Representing the 3D geometry as a level set constructed from Gaussian radial basis functions retains substantial geometric freedom with only a few hundred design variables. This compact representation makes gradient-free optimization practical for fully 3D nanophotonic devices, eliminating the need for adjoint calculations. This unlocks the use of any Maxwell solver or auxiliary algorithms that should express fabrication constraints for which the required derivatives are unavailable or impractical to obtain, and enables embarrassingly parallel workflows. Consequently, binary fabrication requirements, such as structural connectivity, can be rigorously enforced, avoiding the differentiable approximations commonly used in gradient-based optimization. Here, we demonstrate the combination of the gradient-free LSM with a connected-component analysis algorithm to enforce the structural integrity of the design. We demonstrate the applicability of the gradient-free LSM by optimizing a Y-splitter while strictly enforcing the structural integrity of the material and the void in the design.
2611.15656.title: Gradient-Free Inverse Design of 3D Nanophotonic Devices Using the Level-Set-Method

2611.15719.abstract: We study a three-dimensional dynamic thermoplastic system with a temperature-dependent convex yield set whose deviatoric section may collapse completely at a finite temperature. The underlying constitutive model is rate-independent Prandtl-Reuss perfect plasticity, without Kelvin-Voigt viscosity, hardening, or a safe-load condition. We construct global approximation-generated relaxed entropy-energy states by a one-parameter Temam-Norton-Hoff-Galerkin scheme with an undiscretized heat equation and untruncated plastic heat production. The logarithmic temperature is strongly compact in $L^2(0,T;L^q(Ω))$ for every $q<6$ and in $L^p((0,T)\timesΩ)$ for every $p<8/3$. An entropy-weighted work estimate yields convergence of the overstress at rate $O(\sqrt{\log n/n})$ in every fixed finite Lebesgue space and identifies stress admissibility. The constitutive limit comprises a distributional plastic balance, finite support-weighted measures, and compact-fibre lifts carrying exact normality and maximum plastic work. A locally finite lift on the positive-radius fibres unifies the level-restricted limits at every continuity level. At the macroscopic level, however, the available compactness does not identify a canonical stress-plastic-flow pairing. Moreover, an explicit smooth state satisfying the intrinsic relaxed balance conditions shows that these conditions do not imply macroscopic Prandtl-Reuss normality. In the fully collapsed regime, an energy-entropy rigidity argument determines the evolution and yields approximation-generated examples in which the plastic flow need not be a finite measure or the displacement need not retain its full boundary trace. Thermal concentration and plastic entropy production remain explicit throughout.
2611.15719.title: Dynamic Prandtl-Reuss Thermoplasticity with Degenerating Yield Constraints

2611.15806.abstract: Ice formation, a crucial phase transition for life on Earth, mainly occurs through heterogeneous nucleation on a solid substrate. Despite the importance of this phenomenon, the correlation between the structure of the substrate and its ability to induce ice nucleation remains poorly understood. In this work, we use molecular dynamics simulations with an atomistic model of water to investigate how the lattice mismatch affects the ability of the substrate to nucleate ice. To unambiguously quantify the mismatch, we use substrates with a stretched ice structure. We put the substrate in contact with supercooled water and determine the temperature at which ice spontaneously nucleates during the course of the simulations. We find that the nucleation temperature decreases by $\sim$ 5-6 K for each percent by which the substrate lattice is stretched relative to that of ice. This trend is similar to that previously obtained with a coarse-grained water model [Camarillo et al., J. Chem. Phys. 160, 134505 (2024)]. \textcolor{black}{The substrate induces a fluctuating network of subcritical ice-like clusters, from which a spherical-cap-shaped supercritical nucleus eventually emerges stochastically.} Using Classical Nucleation Theory, combine previously reported homogeneous nucleation rates with heterogeneous nucleation rates computed in this work to estimate key heterogeneous nucleation parameters, including the nucleation barrier, the kinetic pre-factor, and the contact angle. The latter is consistent with a microscopic visualization of nucleation trajectories, supporting the applicability of Classical Nucleation Theory to describe a microscopic phenomenon such as heterogeneous ice nucleation.
2611.15806.title: Heterogeneous ice nucleation with TIP4P/Ice: the role of lattice mismatch

2611.15845.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) spin vorticity models (SVMs) have been proposed to realize an exotic 2-form U(1) classical spin liquid (CSL), characterized by a zero-curl constraint, string excitations, and deconfined fluctuating membranes. A previous numerical study [PRB 111, 064417 (2025)] uncovered a puzzle in the pyrochlore lattice SVM: despite exhibiting pinch points characteristic of a U(1) spin liquid, it also develops weak all-in--all-out (AIAO) order. Here, we show that the emergence of the 2-form CSL in 3D SVMs is preempted by an intrinsic instability towards entropy-driven height locking. We establish this by resolving the ground state constraints using a height mapping, which we further relate to a 3-state Potts antiferromagnet. This identifies the pyrochlore's weak AIAO order as permutationally symmetric sublattice (PSS) order, albeit with an exceptionally weak locking strength. We extend the SVM to lattices of corner-sharing octahedra and cubes, where we identify the alternative broken-sublattice-symmetry (BSS) order, a hidden order without magnetic Bragg peaks coexisting with collective paramagnetism. All three models undergo a 3D Ising transition consistent with a symmetry-allowed locking potential in the coarse-grained height theory. The spin liquid persists over intermediate length and temperature scales, but a critical Coulomb ground state ensemble fails to materialize, its correlations cut off by the finite locking length. These findings illustrate how microscopic constraints can determine the ultimate stability of emergent gauge theories in frustrated spin systems.
2611.15845.title: Potts Order Preempts Emergence of 2-Form U(1) Spin Liquidity in Three-Dimensional Spin Vorticity Models

2611.16468.abstract: Data-driven constitutive model discovery is recast as causal discovery of mechanism parent sets using time-unrolled structural causal models. Hard-coding balance laws and constitutive skeletons, candidate graphs score environment--mechanism and state--state edges via weak-form equilibrium gaps evaluated from full-field displacements, avoiding the need to measure stresses or internal variables. An adaptive lasso and a NOTEARS-type constraint ensure graph acyclicity and an explicit evaluation order, treating climate-chamber protocols as interventions. Automatic differentiation yields the score's Gauss--Newton matrix as a local identifiability certificate, driving greedy D-optimal test design. In a synthetic study on a hygro-thermo-viscoelastic damaging plate (8 true edges among 13 candidates), interventional data recover the exact true graph in 7 of 10 runs (0.01px displacement noise) with zero attribution error. Conversely, observational data with a temperature--moisture correlation of $-0.998$ fail entirely because confounded scores are 250--380 times flatter. Observationally discovered models reproduce training climates (3.6% error) but mispredict hot and humid climates by up to 41.5% (16.9% average), whereas interventionally discovered models stay within 3.2%. A correlation sweep shows the certificate successfully predicts attribution errors, though weak-form score noise bias remains a primary limitation. Computed without knowledge of the truth, the D-optimal design selects test sets ranked second or third out of 126 candidates.
2611.16468.title: Physics-constrained differentiable causal discovery of constitutive mechanisms through boundary value problems

2611.16535.abstract: Single-crystal processing of Ni-based superalloys using laser-directed energy deposition (L-DED) is extremely challenging, given the interplay of a number of processing parameters. In this work, we develop strategies to maintain single-crystal growth in long cylindrical rod geometries by combining dynamic adjustment of laser power, informed by in-situ infrared thermal feedback, with a simulation-guided external cooling system. This combined approach ensures optimal heat extraction during additive manufacturing, maintaining near-steady-state conditions at the solidification interface and extending continuous epitaxial growth to nearly twice the build height achievable through process control alone. The developed strategy results in continuous single-crystal growth, as validated by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). The steady-state nature of solidification is revealed through the near-constant primary dendritic arm spacing. Further, the heat-treatment is optimized by reducing the solutionizing time (by 47\%), resulting in faster eutectic dissolution. Comparison of the aged microstructures reveals a similar distribution of precipitates between the classical Bridgman- and L-DED-processed samples.
2611.16535.title: Bulk CMSX-4 Single-Crystal Builds via Laser-Directed Energy Deposition: Epitaxial Stability and Microstructure Evolution

2611.16740.abstract: We study the scattering of topological kinks in a discrete $φ^4$ chain with a localized, adaptive defect, motivated by autonomous self-healing mechanisms in fibrous and polymeric chains. The defect represents damaged flanking bonds whose coupling stiffness evolves dynamically via an internal healing variable, driven by the local energy density and moderated by a viscoelastic relaxation rate $β$. Using high-resolution numerical simulations, we identify a sharp transition at a critical impact velocity $v_c$ separating kink reflection from transmission ($v_c \simeq 0.4183$ for the benchmark initial defect stiffness $C_{\min} = 0.2$). While subcritical kinks ($v_i < v_c$) bounce back with little energy deposition and supercritical ones ($v_i > v_c$) cross the defect too quickly to induce noticeable recovery, kinks near the threshold ($v_i \simeq v_c$) undergo resonant trapping. This prolonged dwell time transfers substantial vibrational energy into the defect, driving the healing variable to nearly full restoration ($h_{\max} \approx 0.98$). Notably, while $v_c$ and the peak defect energy $E_{d,\max}$ depend strongly on $C_{\min}$ and are largely unaffected by $β$, non-zero relaxation ($β> 0$) shortens the trapping window and reduces the final recovery efficiency. Our results show that energy-driven self-healing in discrete lattices is controlled by the cumulative dwell time and time-integrated energy excitation rather than the instantaneous impact peak alone.
2611.16740.title: Near-Threshold Kink Trapping Enhances Defect Healing in an Adaptive $\boldsymbol{φ^4}$ Chain

2611.17254.abstract: Demixing through liquid-liquid phase separation is relevant to nanoparticle (NP) aggregation in polymer nanocomposites (PNCs), biomolecular compartmentalization, and liquids embedded in elastic networks. Mixing-demixing phase behavior depends on factors, such as particle size distribution, system dimen-sionality, intermolecular interactions, and relative concentrations. Here, using Langevin Dynamics simu-lations, we systematically investigate the effect of inter-nanoparticle repulsion on the self-assembly of PNCs under extreme confinement. A nanoparticle assembly, in the form of a compact droplet, is immersed in a polymer matrix of semiflexible, rod-like chains. By varying the nanoparticle-nanoparticle repulsion strength, while fixing all other interactions, we identify four distinct regimes with respect to the self-assembled NP morphologies: droplet, slab, crystalline droplet, and dispersed. Cluster-based analysis reveals a progressive loss of nanoparticle droplet integrity, leading to fragmentation within the dispersed regime. Local order of the nanoparticle assembly and global order of polymer chains are gauged through refined descriptors, quantifying the degrees of crystallinity and of nematic order, respectively. Interest-ingly, the slab regime exhibits negligible nanoparticle crystallization yet demonstrates the strongest polymer nematic ordering. In contrast, the crystalline droplet displays extensive triangular close-packed crystallites accompanied by a significant reduction in polymer nematic order, owing to its rhomboid shape. In the dispersed regime, nanoparticle fragmentation facilitates efficient mixing and local smectic-like ordering of the polymer chains. These findings demonstrate that fine-tuning inter-NP repulsions can control self-organization and the resulting morphologies, providing insights into PNCs with tailored functionality.
2611.17254.title: Inter-Nanoparticle Repulsion Effect on Self-Organization in Polymer Nanocomposites: A Langevin Dynamics Simulation Study

2611.17283.abstract: Ceramic materials that maintain structural integrity and resist thermal-shock under extreme conditions are critical for many applications. Here we show that spark plasma sintered composites containing equal weight fractions of hexagonal silicon carbide (6H-SiC) and boron nitride (h-BN) exhibit exceptional stability under extreme high-temperature oxidizing conditions and unusually stable temperature-independent thermal conductivity across a broad temperature range. Under high-velocity oxygen-fuel torch exposure in air, it withstands prolonged heating and thermal-cycling at surface temperatures reaching >1500 °C, whereas pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractures or erodes. Microstructural evaluation shows the formation of a multi-phase surface silica layer that further protects the material from oxidation. Finite-element analysis heat-flux map shows that intrinsic porosity mitigates thermal stress, while ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations reveal thermally driven interfacial reconstruction and the formation of a Si-N/C-B-rich bonding network, enhancing the interfacial cohesion at elevated temperatures. This lightweight, easily machinable ceramic composite will be a promising structural material in extreme environment applications.
2611.17283.comment: 76 Pages, 4 Main Figures, 30 SI Figures, 8 Tables, Authors version, Comments are welcome
2611.17283.title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability

2611.17498.abstract: Obtaining accurate and analytically tractable closed-form expressions for complex physical systems remains a fundamental challenge in statistical mechanics. In this work, we investigate three approximation problems in polymer statistical mechanics using two complementary symbolic regression frameworks: Deep Symbolic Optimization (DSO), based on reinforcement learning, and PyOperon, based on genetic programming with nonlinear least-squares constant optimization.   First, for the force-extension relationship of the Worm-Like Chain (WLC) model, DSO achieves a maximum relative error below 0.15%, while PyOperon reduces it to 0.05%, outperforming the Marko-Siggia formula (approximately 17%) and the Petrosyan approximation. Second, for the logarithmic factorial, ln(n!), both frameworks recover the dominant structure of Stirling's formula directly from analytical data. Using residual learning on a continued-fraction expansion of the Stirling remainder, PyOperon reduces the maximum relative error by a factor of 1.3 x 10^4 compared with the most accurate of nine classical approximations for n in [1, 30]. Third, for the non-Gaussian radial probability density of the Freely Jointed Chain (FJC) model, physics-informed residual learning improves the approximation by factors of 11.2 over Darabi et al. (2023) and 4.6 over the steepest-descent approximation.   The discovered expressions remain analytically tractable across all three applications. These results demonstrate the complementary capabilities of DSO and PyOperon for discovering accurate closed-form approximations in statistical and continuum mechanics.
2611.17498.title: New Closed-Form Approximations in Statistical Mechanics Obtained by Symbolic Regression

2611.17638.abstract: Personalized bioelectronic devices for wound therapy require not only conformal fabrication on complex body surfaces but also functional adaptation of their electrical characteristics to individual wound geometries. Here, we present an AI-guided robotic in situ printing platform for fabricating wireless wound electrotherapy devices directly on transparent wound dressings. The system integrates a 3D vision camera, a six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, direct-ink-writing, and geometry-aware RF design optimization. AI-based wound segmentation is used to determine wound dimensions and local surface curvature, while the reconstructed three-dimensional geometry is incorporated into the electromagnetic design of the receiving coil and interdigitated electrodes. In contrast to conventional approaches that use surface geometry only for trajectory generation, the proposed method accounts for both anatomical curvature and tissue dielectric loading to compensate for geometry-induced shifts in resonant behavior. A printable silver ink was characterized in terms of rheology, dimensional reproducibility, electrical resistance, and electromechanical stability, and was used to fabricate multilayer wireless devices directly on curved polyurethane dressings. Wireless power transfer, impedance characteristics, and electric-field delivery were evaluated experimentally and numerically. Finally, robotic in situ fabrication was demonstrated on an anthropomorphic tissue-equivalent forearm phantom, where the measured dielectric properties of the phantom were incorporated into the RF optimization, enabling resonant operation near the target frequency of 25 MHz. This work establishes a perception-to-design-to-fabrication framework for geometry-adaptive wireless bioelectronics and provides a technological foundation for future physical-AI-enabled manufacturing of personalized on-body electrotherapy devices.
2611.17638.title: AI-guided robotic in situ fabrication of curvature- and tissue-adaptive wireless bioelectronics

2611.17650.abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $β$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.
2611.17650.title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation

2611.17655.abstract: Neural quantum states and tensor networks have emerged as leading techniques for simulating quantum many-body systems. However, disordered systems remain extremely challenging in both frameworks as they require computation of the ground state for every realization of the disorder. Recently, neural quantum states have been used to construct foundation models that generate the ground state directly from the Hamiltonian. Still, they are hindered by the need to perform extensive sampling to estimate observables. To address these difficulties, we introduce the foundation tensor network (FTN), which uses a neural network to generate the tensor network representation of the ground-state wavefunction from the Hamiltonian. To accelerate training, we develop a technique, called \texttt{GridBP}, based on iterated one-dimensional belief propagation that reduces the cost of computing the energy expectation value to just two tensor contractions. We use FTNs to calculate the critical parameters of the glass transition in the quantum Edwards-Anderson model via finite-size scaling analysis. To facilitate rapid averaging, we use a moment-generating function to evaluate the order parameter, lowering the cost to a single tensor contraction. We obtain high-fidelity estimates for the critical parameters by averaging over 500,000 disorder realizations.
2611.17655.title: Foundation Tensor Networks Generalize Across Lattice Hamiltonians

2611.17794.abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.
2611.17794.title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing

2611.17976.abstract: Magnetocardiography (MCG) noninvasively measures cardiac magnetic fields. Conventional cryogenic systems use fixed multichannel arrays, whereas room-temperature sensors enable flexible placement to reduce array size and measurement redundancy. The present study aims at developing a scheme to identify the optimal sensor placements by utilizing three methodological sensor optimization frameworks such as physics driven, experimental data driven and a hybrid combination of both. The physics-driven method optimizes continuous planar coordinates using D-optimality, spatial correlation, and leastsquares error. The data-driven method uses measured spatiotemporal fields and pole-geometry metrics, while the hybrid method integrates both approaches. The evaluation is performed using training objective, Pearson correlation, normalized root-meansquare error (NRMSE) and pole separation(mm), orientation(°) and trajectory(mm) errors, where physics-driven optimization identified 16 sensors with a correlation of 0.9914 and an NRMSE of 0.0139, with pole separation, orientation, and trajectory errors of 3.71 mm, 1.38°, and 3.55 mm, respectively. Data-driven optimization shows diminishing improvements beyond 17 sensors, achieving correlation 0.9840, NRMSE 0.0035, and pole errors of approximately 4.30 mm, 1.70°, and 6.80 mm. The hybrid method achieves correlation 0.9945 and NRMSE 0.0201 with 14 sensors, reducing sensor count by 12.5% relative to the physics-driven configuration. Its pole errors of 6.50 mm, 2.31°, and 7.50 mm satisfy the study-defined thresholds, balancing array compactness with magnetic-field morphology preservation. These results show that optimized placement helps alleviate the complexity of data redundancy and enhances the performance of MCG as a routine cost-effective clinical measurement.
2611.17976.title: A Multiobjective Optimization Framework for Sensor Array Design in Magnetocardiography

2611.18236.abstract: Eukaryotic initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) drives cap-dependent translation, regulated by 4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) competing for its dorsal and lateral surfaces. CYFIP1, a scaffold protein, is both a WAVE Regulatory Complex component and a non-canonical 4E-BP repressing translation via a short helical motif, linked to autism spectrum disorders and cancer. Prior work modeled only this isolated motif as a peptide, leaving the full interface uncharacterized. Starting from this preliminary evidence, we modeled the full-length proteins as flexible partners: all-atom simulations fed a data-driven docking search (HADDOCK3), which guided funnel-restrained Temperature-Accelerated Molecular Dynamics of a coarse-grained Martini 3 representation. Ten replicas accumulated 100 $μ$s of enhanced sampling. Funnel-restraint variables efficiently sample binding and unbinding but are structurally degenerate: direct clustering of the raw trajectory collapses these poses into poorly resolved groups. We instead reweighted the biased trajectories onto a contact-based latent space built by benchmarking PCA against a beta-Variational Autoencoder, then clustered minima of the equilibrium free-energy surface: only intermediate regularization resolved distinct, homogeneous modes. Three such modes recur, engaging eIF4E's canonical dorsal site, its non-canonical lateral site, and both. We find that CYFIP1 also engages eIF4E through a second surface, the same that mediates its WAVE-complex dimerization, and a basic patch. Both plausibly explain residual binding previously reported after motif mutation. This suggests its translational and cytoskeletal roles compete for the same surface. Most contacts on eIF4E fall outside this dorsal/lateral interface. This heterogeneous, plastic ensemble offers a structural basis for mutagenesis and therapeutic peptide design.
2611.18236.title: Deciphering multiple binding modes in large protein complexes via Enhanced Sampling and beta-VAE: the CYFIP1-eIF4E case

2611.18435.abstract: Local parts of a closed, non-equilibrium quantum many-body system can reach stationarity through the buildup of entanglement between different regions. In this paper we investigate how this process is affected by the presence of a quantum impurity that breaks a global symmetry of the bulk. In particular, we study a charged dual-unitary quantum circuit perturbed by a symmetry-breaking, non-dual-unitary gate acting on a spatially fixed pair of sites. In this setup we calculate the entanglement entropy for a subsystem that does not contain the impurity, as well as the mutual information and logarithmic negativity for a bipartite subsystem that straddles the impurity. We obtain exact results in the early time regime for these quantities from the dual unitarity of the bulk system. Beyond this regime, we compute the predictions of the quasiparticle and entanglement membrane pictures, supporting them with exact calculations obtained by taking the corresponding limits of the bulk entangling power. We find that the presence of a symmetry-breaking impurity can lead to a richer behaviour of quantum relaxation, including non-monotonic evolution of the entanglement entropy, a modification of the long-time steady state, and persistent subsystem mutual information and entanglement negativity. This behaviour is understood in terms of long-range correlations generated by scattering from the impurity, and facilitated by the ballistic propagation of the conserved charges.
2611.18435.title: Entanglement and information dynamics in charged dual-unitary circuits with impurities

2611.18447.abstract: Nesting in powder bed fusion (PBF), an additive manufacturing (AM) process, determines the positions and orientations of parts within the build space and influences build height and build time. As the number of parts and feasible placements increases, the nesting problem becomes computationally demanding. Exact approaches are limited to small problem sizes as computational effort increases rapidly with the problem size, while heuristic and metaheuristic approaches involve a trade-off between solution quality and computation time. Quantum annealing (QA) offers an alternative for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its application to nesting in AM remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a QA-based approach for nesting in AM to investigate its feasibility and its scaling behavior across three problem sizes. An iterative binary quadratic model based approach (IBQM) is developed to minimize build height while considering the geometric characteristics of AM parts. Geometric abstraction, iterative decomposition, and variable pruning are applied to address the computational complexity of the nesting problem. The approach is evaluated using three cases with increasing problem sizes and compared to a classical approach combining tabu search and simulated annealing (TBSA). Compared with TBSA, IBQM reduces the build height of the original parts by up to 13.32% and the computation time by up to 74.27%.
2611.18447.title: Nesting in additive manufacturing using quantum annealing

2611.18783.abstract: We present a unified continuum framework that combines chemotactic feedback with motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) to investigate the physical origin of aggregation in self-secreting cell populations. While classical Keller-Segel theory attributes pattern formation to chemotactic instabilities, we show that this mechanism breaks down in systems with proportional density-dependent (autocrine) production and uptake: linear stability analysis reveals that chemical fluctuations decouple from density, eliminating chemotactic aggregation at leading order. In contrast, introducing density-dependent motility restores instability through a purely mechanical mechanism corresponding to MIPS. Our results demonstrate that chemotactic feedback does not alter the nature of this instability, but instead enhances its growth rate and accelerates aggregation. This unifies two central paradigms of biological self-organization and revises the role of chemotaxis in collective cell migration.
2611.18783.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Manuscript is submitted and currently under review
2611.18783.title: Motility-induced phase separation drives aggregation in chemotactic systems

2611.18795.abstract: The intrinsic thermal conductivity ($κ$) of graphene remains highly controversial because of physical and metrological complexities. Although the thermal bridge method enables reliable measurements, sample fabrication remains challenging. Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $μ$m. Suspended BLG with unavoidable polymer residues exhibits length-independent thermal conductivity of approximately 570 W/(m K) at room temperature, remaining nearly constant from 250 to 350 K and robust to rigorous surface cleaning and amorphous silicon nitride substrates. Homogeneous non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) simulations show that amorphous carbon coverage of only approximately 0.01 monolayer is sufficient to suppress out-of-plane flexural acoustic (ZA) phonons. These findings challenge the prevailing view that rigid substrates suppress ZA phonons more strongly than surface contamination and identify a robust lower bound of $κ$ governed by amorphous surface scattering. This lower bound reflects heat conduction in graphene under realistic device conditions and provides a reference for fundamental phonon transport studies and the integration of graphene into thermal management applications in electronic devices and chips.
2611.18795.comment: 4 figures in the main text; Supporting Information included in the PDF
2611.18795.title: Lower Bound of Thermal Conductivity in Graphene

2611.19060.abstract: Coupled precipitation and interfacial segregation in low-alloy steels change precipitate stability and morphology, which influence strengthening and embrittlement. Cu-rich precipitates (CRPs) and Mn-Ni-Si-rich precipitates (MNSPs) frequently form core-shell or appendage morphologies, but the interfacial energetics controlling this change are not well quantified. We combine a density-functional-theory-trained cluster expansion with lattice Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the Fe/CRP, Fe/MNSP and Cu/MNSP interfaces within one Hamiltonian. The three coefficients based on excess internal energy follow gamma_Cu/MNSP < gamma_Fe/CRP <~ gamma_Fe/MNSP and give a positive work of adhesion and a negative spreading parameter, consistent with favorable Mn-Ni-Si attachment to a CRP and partial coverage. Only Ni segregates to the Fe/CRP boundary. Mn and Si segregate weakly on their own but become more enriched when Ni is present and co-segregate with Ni at the boundary. Ni forms an interfacial layer about one monolayer thick with an excess of 7.4-9.6 atoms/nm^2, develops B2-like local order and shows an energy reduction that increases with Ni coverage. At 1 at.% matrix Ni, a Gibbs adsorption analysis gives a Fe/CRP free-energy reduction of about 0.15 J/m^2. These interface coefficients and segregation trends connect segregation, interface energy and co-precipitation and support compositional optimization in low-alloy steels.
2611.19060.comment: 43 pages, 13 figures, 1 table (main text); supplementary information included at the end (8 figures, 4 tables)
2611.19060.title: Interplay of interfacial energetics and selective Ni segregation in the morphology of co-precipitates in low-alloy steels

2611.19334.abstract: We propose a Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework to quantify the intrinsic (aleatoric) uncertainty in a continuous-variable quantum random number generator (CV-QRNG). This provides a direct data-driven measure of the QRNG's randomness generation. The BNN is trained on raw homodyne voltage time-series data from a fiber-coupled vacuum-fluctuation QRNG (VFQRNG). For each voltage data segment, the network predicts a Gaussian distribution (mean and variance) for the next sample, and the ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as a diagnostic of entropy-related behavior under assumptions of our quantum source model. Thus, the predicted variance serves as a BNN model-based monitor of the randomness-generation process. We validate that the BNN metric increases with the local-oscillator (LO) power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy (extractable randomness). We also show the metric is sensitive to practical imperfections, coarse-graining (simulating limited analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sampling) or reducing ADC bit depth causes a clear drop in predicted aleatoric uncertainty, consistent with the source min-entropic model. These results establish the BNN-based metric as a complementary, physically motivated diagnostic tool for QRNG characterization. Unlike conventional tests (e.g. autocorrelation) that miss hardware issues like low ADC resolution, our method provides a direct real-time monitor of the VFRNG performance. Therefore, this metric is useful for real-time monitoring of CV-QRNG conditions, including drifts and other imperfections.
2611.19334.title: Study of Randomness in Quantum Random Number Generator using Bayesian Neural Networks

2611.19342.abstract: DNA--protein co-condensation is an important regulatory mechanism for gene expression and repair. For straight DNA under constant stretching forces, co-condensation is ``all-or-nothing'': above a critical force, condensates are prevented from nucleating, while below it the entire molecule collapses into a droplet. Here we show by coarse-grained simulations and analytic theory that DNA supercoiling mechanically differentiates the condensation substrate: DNA plectonemes constitute force-insulated pockets on which condensates can nucleate even above the critical force. The size of the resulting droplets is tunable through the applied force and linking number. Surface tension drives the coarsening of multiple plectoneme-associated condensates into a single topological droplet. Magnetic tweezers experiments with spermine reproduce both the force-dependent collapse and the supercoiling-dependent condensation.
2611.19342.title: Tunable topological droplets on supercoiled DNA under tension

2611.19591.abstract: Methods for reliable in-situ estimation of small-strain damping ratio remain far less developed than those for in-situ shear wave velocity (Vs) measurements. For surface wave-based approaches, challenges with extracting damping ratios are caused by both difficulties associated with developing attenuation coefficients from recorded wavefields and complexities involved when interpreting their multimodal irregularities during inversion. This study presents a joint inversion framework for extracting shear damping ratio (Ds0) and Vs profiles from Rayleigh-wave attenuation and phase velocity data using a viscoelastic predominant-mode approach. Unlike conventional inversion, the proposed formulation identifies the mode contributing most strongly to the measured wavefield, allowing multimodal attenuation and dispersion data to be incorporated without explicit modal indexing. This approach has significant benefits for inverting attenuation data, whose modal behavior is much more irregular than phase velocity. A coupled inversion strategy is adopted to jointly estimate the Vs and Ds0 while addressing their different sensitivities to phase velocity and attenuation. The predominant-mode attenuation concept is first validated against two synthetic ground models of increasing complexity. The synthetic inversion results demonstrate the framework's ability to recover the Ds0 and Vs profiles and capture modal transitions associated with a low-velocity layer. The framework is then applied to active-source field data from Mirandola, Italy, where the fundamental mode dominates, and Bird's Landing, California, where a soft peat layer produces significant higher-modes. At both sites, the inverted Vs profiles agreed well with independent site characterization data, while the damping estimates exhibit physically plausible trends and provide site-specific information that complements empirical estimates.
2611.19591.title: Extracting Damping Ratio and Shear Wave Velocity through Joint Inversion of Rayleigh Wave Attenuation and Phase Velocity Data

2611.19658.abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.
2611.19658.title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

2611.19676.abstract: Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.
2611.19676.title: Score-Based Stochastic Closure Modeling via Offline Indirect Learning and Online Data Assimilation

2611.19693.abstract: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy.
