We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature. The database provides a systematic reference for metallic coherent heterophase interfaces and demonstrates the importance of separating strain and chemical energy contributions when interpreting alloy behavior.
2611.19693.comment: Main manuscript: 32 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Supporting Information: 31 pages, 22 figures, 4 tables
2611.19693.title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions

2611.20002.abstract: Recently, Thomas et al. [Nanoscale 17, 18291 (2025)] showed that bismuth oxido nanoclusters (BiO-NCs) of the type [Bi$_{38}$ O$_{45}$ (Boc-L-Phe-O)$_{24}$] form chains when deposited onto gold or pyrolitic graphite substrates. This chain formation is significantly enhanced when the bismuth in the BiO-NCs is partially replaced by cerium through doping. In this work, we study a simplified, coarse-grained model of this process, namely (magnetic) Stockmayer particles in the presence of an attractive substrate. The model is investigated by means of molecular dynamics simulations. The deposition experiment is mimicked by a rapid quench from high temperature to a low temperature below the bulk coexistence curve. The results are found to be qualitatively similar to the experimental observations reported earlier. In our simulations, we find significant chain formation in the bulk even at rather low concentrations, which is in contrast to the BiO-NCs in ethanol for which dynamic light scattering reveals negligible aggregation in the absence of the substrate. This lends support to a scenario, conjectured in the work of Thomas at al., where the dipole moments are induced by the particle-substrate interaction and hence there is little dipole moment in the bulk. In a second part, we study the system in equilibrium. We consider the scaling of chains, the number of layers populated as a function of two-dimensional density, and we draw analogies to polymers on interfaces, which have been extensively studied over the past decades. Most notably, it is found that the chains behave as self-avoiding walks at low densities, which gives way to rod-like scaling at higher densities.
2611.20002.title: Self-assembly of dipolar nanoclusters on an attractive substrate: A coarse-grained simulation approach

2611.20281.abstract: Compliant coatings offer a passive approach to modifying near-wall turbulence and potentially reducing skin-friction drag, but high-fidelity exploration of the coupled parameter space is costly. We develop a two-way coupled resolvent-Galerkin framework for turbulent channel flow over finite-thickness, layered viscoelastic coatings. The fluid is modeled using the Navier-Stokes equations linearized about a turbulent mean state, while the solid is represented by a through-thickness Galerkin discretization of the elastodynamic equations. The solid response is condensed into a spectral surface-impedance operator at the fluid-solid interface. At $Re_τ= 180$, stiff panels approach the rigid-wall response, whereas more compliant panels modify the low-rank response associated with the near-wall cycle. A Reynolds-number study shows that panels with fixed nondimensional material stiffness can produce different responses depending on whether their thickness scales with inner or outer flow length scales. The influence of viscoelastic damping is examined across low- and high-frequency regimes, where stiffness-proportional damping alters the high-frequency fractional-energy distribution, while the low-frequency distribution remains relatively insensitive to damping. For multilayer panels, the fluid-facing material determines the interfacial wave speed, while the subsurface stiffness distribution modifies the panel's effective thickness. Temporal stability analysis identifies regions of parameter space where a steady harmonic response is relevant and regions where instabilities grow. Finally, a leading-order, covariance-based drag-estimation framework relates the coupled response to changes in the mean flow and to the estimated skin-friction drag. Together, these tools provide a basis for screening coating designs and selecting candidates for high-fidelity simulations and experiments.
2611.20281.title: Resolvent-based modeling of turbulent flow over multilayer compliant surfaces

2611.20429.abstract: FiuMD is a GPU molecular dynamics engine that advances many independent biomolecular simulations as a single batch, even when the systems differ in size, topology, force-field parameters, periodic box, timestep, or thermostat parameters. All systems are concatenated into global tensors, so the classical interaction terms and a shared TorchMD-Net neural network potential are evaluated for the whole batch at once, while each system keeps its own integration and thermostat. FiuMD started as a fork of TorchMD and reworks its system representation, force evaluation, and integration to handle such heterogeneous batches. We test it with coarse-grained C$α$ models of chignolin, Trp-cage, BBL, and $λ$-repressor. In double precision, forces within a heterogeneous batch agree with isolated FiuMD and TorchMD evaluations to within the precision of repeated evaluations, with a maximum relative difference of $7\times10^{-16}$ across 60 systems. Over 1000 steps without a thermostat, batched trajectories deviate by at most $2.5\times10^{-11}$ Angstrom from isolated ones, even when periodic images lie within the neural network cutoff. With a different target temperature for each system of the ensemble, the mean and width of each system's kinetic temperature match the values expected from its own thermostat. We show that when individual simulations are too small to fill the GPU, batching can improve throughput several-fold over TorchMD. On a single GPU, batching four different protein systems achieves a 4.6-7.8-fold speedup per step compared with sequential TorchMD simulations. Compared with sequential homogeneous FiuMD batches, heterogeneous batching provides up to a 4-fold speedup for smaller batches while maintaining comparable performance for larger ones.
2611.20429.title: FiuMD: Heterogeneous Batching for Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics with Neural Network Potentials

2611.20525.abstract: The elastic effect on the stability of boundary layers is studied for incompressible elastic fluids in the half-plane. It is known from [33] that if the deformation tensor matrix is nonsingular near the boundary, elasticity can prevent the formation of a boundary layer. In this paper, we prove stability properties when the deformation tensor degenerates. Our results are twofold: (1) when the first row of the deformation tensor has a non-degenerate projection onto a fixed direction, the initial-boundary value problem for the two-dimensional viscoelastic Prandtl boundary layer equations in the half-plane admits local well-posedness in Sobolev spaces, without any monotonicity condition on the velocity profile; (2) when the first row of the deformation tensor vanishes simultaneously at one point, the linearized Prandtl boundary layer system is ill-posed. The first result reveals the stabilizing effect of elasticity against the classical Prandtl instability. The second result shows that elastic effects cannot suppress the Prandtl-type instability associated with a non-degenerate critical point of the velocity profile.
2611.20525.title: Effects of elasticity on the stability of viscoelastic boundary layers

2611.20555.abstract: Many biological and engineered filaments exhibit internal structure or fluidity that alters their elastic behavior. We study the elasticity of microscale filamentous smectic condensates, grown during liquid-liquid crystal phase separation. We use a Fourier analysis of their thermal bend fluctuations to measure their persistence length, which follows a non-classic linear scaling with their cross-sectional area, in contrast to the classic quadratic scaling for elastic filaments. We rationalize this scaling using the Helfrich energy to compute the free energy of bending a filament with internal smectic fluid ordering. Our analysis then provides a direct method to measure the bend modulus K, which quantifies the rigidity of smectic layers; providing the first method to directly measure K for dispersed smectic phases. We quantify the softening of filaments in the presence of shorter alkyl-tail mesogen dopants, decreasing K by up to ~35%. Out results suggest how nanoscale smectic organization and molecular composition determine filament-scale elasticity, informing the control of filament mechanics and self-assembly in biomimetic and engineered materials.
2611.20555.title: Bending Rigidity of Smectic Filaments

2611.20624.abstract: A low-cost, miniaturized, additively manufactured transmissive linear-to-circular polarization converter for L-band air and space communication systems is presented. The proposed polarizer employs an in-house-fabricated high-permittivity dielectric medium, realized using a 3-D printed polylactic acid (PLA) enclosure filled with a TiO$_2$--water mixture. Variation in the effective permittivity is achieved by adjusting the mixture filling fraction. The selected 60\% filling fraction corresponds to an effective relative permittivity of 11.3 at 1 GHz. The high-permittivity loading enables miniaturization of the polarizer height and area by reducing the anisotropic dielectric unit-cell dimensions to $\boldsymbol{0.037λ_0 \times 0.037λ_0 \times 0.22λ_0}$. An additively manufactured polarizer with overall dimensions $\boldsymbol{0.83λ_0 \times 0.77λ_0 \times 0.22λ_0}$ is experimentally validated using a compact linearly polarized feed source. The measured results demonstrate LP-to-CP conversion, with a 3 dB axial ratio of 12\% and insertion loss of less than 0.6 dB. Radiation-pattern measurements at 1 GHz show LHCP-to-RHCP discrimination levels of 19 and 24 dB in the \textbf{\textit{xz}}- and \textbf{\textit{yz}}-planes, respectively. The proposed configuration combines miniaturization, LP-to-CP conversion, and low-cost additive manufacturing, making it promising for UAV-mounted and other size-constrained L-band satellite communication terminals.
2611.20624.title: Miniaturized Low-Cost 3-D Printed High-Permittivity Dielectric Transmissive LP-to-CP Converter for L-Band Satellite Communications

2611.20857.abstract: Hydrogels are biocompatible smart materials comprised of a hydrophilic polymer network which can absorb a large volume of water (swelling). The changes in shape the gel undergoes as it swells or de-swells can be utilised in the design of actuators. This is of particular interest for many applications whereby hydrogel actuators would be combined into a complex origami-inspired structure which can fold and unfold according to application needs. In this paper, we therefore focus on one such actuator design, the bilayer hinge, which can induce bending (for potential use in a fold/unfold mechanism). We develop a model using the gel lattice spring method (gLSM) which can be used to simulate composite structures comprised of hydrogel and elastomer and compute the equilibrium bending angle of bilayer hinges for a range of geometries and material properties.
2611.20857.title: Will it bend? Modelling hydrogel box hinges with a gel Lattice Spring Method

2611.21022.abstract: The degree of polarisation correlation of the two annihilation photons, measured by Compton polarimetry, has been proposed as a PET biomarker of tissue microstructure, but the statistics it requires have not been quantified. We parameterise the measurement by the linear-polarisation correlation coefficient $κ$ ($κ=1$ maximally entangled, $1/2$ separable), derive the classical Fisher information of double-Compton events and compare it with the quantum Fisher information, relate $κ$ to the annihilation channels of positronium in tissue, and simulate pixelated CdZnTe (CZT) rings. The model is checked against three published measurements and an independent GATE/Geant4 simulation. A double-Compton event carries at most 0.12-0.14 units of Fisher information about $κ$ and 0.015 on average, 0.1-0.6% of the quantum limit. Event-wise maximum likelihood reaches the Cramer-Rao bound, whereas the conventional ratio R needs 1.2-2.3 times more events. The observed coefficient is $κ_{obs}=1-α(1-κ_{pick})$, with a pick-off share $α$ of 0.13-0.29 in tissue; it is sensitive to lipid fraction but not to oxygen, and carries no tissue information if pick-off photons are maximally entangled. Published porous-polymer data imply $κ_{pick}$ = 0.34-0.58. In a 15-mm CZT module, ordering ambiguity, position errors and electron transport roughly halve the information per event, and sequence reconstruction of multi-site events recovers this loss. With $^{18}$F and an eight-module ring, $κ$ can be measured to $\pm0.01$ in a 10-mm tumour, but separating tissues by $κ$ alone requires 6-74 times more decays than are available.
2611.21022.title: How many events does entanglement-based positronium imaging need? Information limits of Compton polarimetry with CZT detectors

2611.21087.abstract: Inertialess elastic instabilities can profoundly affect transport in complex-fluid flows, from mixing in microfluidic devices and displacement through porous media to polymer processing. While such instabilities are well understood in flows with curved streamlines, their origin in rectilinear flows like the prototypical Kolmogorov flow remains unresolved. Here, we report the first experimental evidence of the center-mode elastic instability, at vanishing inertia, in a confined quasi-two-dimensional viscoelastic Kolmogorov flow, driven by electromagnetic forcing. The instability is characterized by the emergence of "arrow-shaped" structures in the velocity field, which fluctuates chaotically as the forcing strength increases. We reproduce these observations in simulations of the Oldroyd-B model and trace the dynamics in the confined flow to the travelling arrowhead structures that emerge from the center-mode instability of unbounded Kolmogorov flow. Our work establishes a generic route to purely elastic instability in rectilinear flows, broadening the conditions under which elastic turbulence and enhanced mixing can arise.
2611.21087.title: Experimental Evidence of Elastic Instability in Viscoelastic Kolmogorov Flow

2611.21281.abstract: Solar-matter interactions are important in many scientific and engineering applications. Modeling them needs consistent optical and thermal-radiative properties over the full solar spectrum. Here we present SpaderOptics, a database for 21 materials: metals, oxides, semiconductors, polymers, ceramics, and carbon. It compiles wavelength-dependent refractive indices and extinction coefficients from the literature. Each literature source is kept separate, together with its original conditions. One physics-based calculation chain turns these data into reflectivity, transmissivity, absorptivity, and emissivity for different incidence angles, slab thicknesses, and temperatures. Combined with the Air Mass Zero (AM0) solar spectrum, the properties give absorbed, reflected, and transmitted solar flux for concentrated sunlight. Equilibrium temperatures are given for both a theoretical lumped body and for a slab body, in which thermal conduction is considered. All data are limited to the solid state, up to a material-specific upper temperature limit. Currently, the database applies to extraterrestrial (AM0) sunlight only. A graphical App is also provided for exploring and visualizing the database.
2611.21281.title: A database of optical and thermal-radiative behaviour of materials under solar radiation

2611.21322.abstract: Global full-waveform inversion (FWI) has matured significantly in recent years, but resolution in the southern hemisphere often remains limited due to sparse receiver coverage. To address this problem, we constructed RevealLO, a global-scale FWI model that updates its predecessor REVEAL by expanding the inversion time window from 1 hour to 3.5 hours. The extended time window incorporates both minor-arc ($R_1, G_1$) and major-arc ($R_2, G_2$) surface wave arrivals, as well as late-arriving multi-orbit body waves, thereby increasing azimuthal coverage beneath ocean basins and the southern hemisphere. We simulate 3-D viscoelastic wavefields using the spectral-element solver Salvus on global fourth-order cubed-sphere meshes, and update velocity structure by successively broadening the period band from 100 - 200 s to 60 - 200 s. Measurements and adjoint sources are based on time-frequency phase misfits, which are suitable for both large-amplitude surface and low-amplitude multiply-reflected body waves. For iterative optimization, we employ a mini-batch stochastic trust-region L-BFGS algorithm, followed by mesh reprojection onto the $33~s$ REVEAL baseline mesh and lowermost-mantle regularization. RevealLO preserves short-period whole-Earth body wave fits while improving azimuthal sampling and mitigating trade-offs between unmodeled azimuthal anisotropy and isotropic structure in the upper and mid mantle.
2611.21322.title: RevealLO: Global-Scale FWI Including Long-Period Major-Arc Surface Wave and Multi-Orbit Body Wave Data

2611.21855.abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erdős-Rényi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.
2611.21855.title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks

2611.21898.abstract: Aggregate molecular systems are routinely understood by decomposing them into local structural units, such as monomers in J/H-aggregates, chemical moieties, motifs, and functional groups. Implicit in such decompositions is the assumption that these local structures remain meaningful within the aggregate. Here, we ask how the symmetries of constituent structures relate to aggregate symmetry, and how this relation determines the constraints that global symmetry imposes on transitions between local symmetry sectors. We construct a covariant local-to-global representation from framed local symmetry data and show that its reconstruction map intertwines with a global quantum representation. By identifying which global symmetry sectors overlap each local symmetry sector, we resolve symmetry-enforced dynamical exclusions into site-resolved pathways. Through Frobenius reciprocity, these exclusions can be determined from standard character tables of the local and global symmetry groups, with the character values in the inner product paired according to the relative positions and orientations of local structures within the aggregate. Although motivated by molecular aggregates, the construction is formulated for arbitrary geometries modeled by a homogeneous space of an ambient transformation group.
2611.21898.title: A Geometric Framework for Local-to-Global Symmetry: Global Constraints on Local Dynamics

2611.22573.abstract: This work explores how the initial free carrier density governs the formation and coherent propagation of Low Spatial Frequency Laser-Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LSF-LIPSS). As a paradigm we have analyzed the behavior of ad-hoc-doped ZnO films. ZnO is a multifunctional Transparent Conducting Oxide (TCO) with many scientific and technologic uses including applications in biomedicine, photonics, sensing or photocatalysis. Many of them would benefit from the use of large area, electrically anisotropic surfaces. By introducing small amounts of Yb3+ as donor dopant in ZnO films grown by Pulse Laser Deposition (PLD), we have substantially improved its carrier density at room temperature (RT) and its electrical conductivity while preserving the functional properties of pure ZnO. For RT carrier densities ne > 1019 cm-3, coherent propagation of LSF-LIPSS has been successfully achieved upon irradiation with 350 fs laser pulses at 1030 nm at high repetition rate (500 kHz) and for laser scanning speeds well above 1 m/s. However, the ablation mechanism (ZnO sublimation at the LIPSS valleys) and the large melting temperature of ZnO, make the thermal conductivity of the substrate, the film thickness and the irradiation pulse duration to play a crucial role in determining the morphology of the LSF-LIPPS propagated over large areas, especially in avoiding film cracking. The results achieved upon optimization fully confirm the role of free carrier density in the large-scale propagation of high quality LSF-LIPSS in doped ZnO and enable using these structures to easily generate large electrical anisotropies over macroscopic regions with conductivities along the LIPSS several times larger than transversally.
2611.22573.title: Targeted material doping to enable the formation and coherent propagation of Laser Induced Periodic Surface Structures (LIPSS): the ZnO paradigm

2611.22902.abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.
2611.22902.title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems

2611.22966.abstract: While polymer adsorption is theoretically well established on flat surfaces --- and somewhat understood on rough surfaces --- the common and practically relevant case of nearly flat stepped surfaces remains poorly studied. Here, we address this gap via extensive simulations of flexible polymer chains grafted at the step edge of vicinal surfaces. For wide terraces, the polymer-step interaction yields a stable step-attached (SA) phase, alongside the desorbed and terrace-adsorbed (TA) phases, all of them separated by continuous transition lines that meet at a multicritical point previously unanticipated in polymer thermodynamics. This scenario is observed for terrace widths $\mathcal{W} \gtrsim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, being $R_g^{(2D)}$ the radius of gyration of TA polymers. Simpler phase diagrams, absent this multicriticality, are found for $\mathcal{W} \lesssim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, where a simple crossover exists between the SA and TA phases. The presence of kinks at the steps does not alter these behaviors. Besides their theoretical relevance, these findings unveil an interesting route to produce polymer nanowires and control polymer conformation via step attachment-detachment on designed stepped surfaces.
2611.22966.title: Polymer adsorption on vicinal surfaces

2611.22983.abstract: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) enables complex multi-layer microfluidic devices, but the physical synthesis of passive-flow designs remains a key bottleneck. In such systems, designers must encode timing synchronization and target dosing directly into channel geometry, even though the available routing space across multiple 3D layers is often highly congested, which makes scaling to complex designs difficult. Existing approaches formulate placement, routing, and fluidic constraints as a single monolithic optimization, leading to combinatorial explosion and poor performance on complex designs. This paper presents a volumetric-aware two-stage synthesis framework that decouples global structure from routing detail. A Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) model first computes a compact multi-layer placement, followed by a dynamic 3D routing engine that enforces timing and volumetric constraints during path construction. To further improve routability in dense layouts, we introduce a hierarchical conflict resolution strategy combining local rip-up-and-reroute with controlled global expansion. Experimental results show that, under timing and volumetric constraints, 3D-VASE consistently improves synthesis speed and, in most test cases, also improves layout quality. Notably, for difficult large-scale cases where prior methods often failed to return any solution within the time limit, 3D-VASE produces feasible high-quality layouts within practical runtimes. These advances enable fast, iterative design-space exploration for complex 3D-printed microfluidic systems.
2611.22983.comment: Accepted for publication in the 32nd Asia and South Pacific Design Automation Conference (ASP-DAC 2027)
2611.22983.title: 3D-VASE: Volumetric-Aware Scalable and Efficient Multi-Layer Design Synthesis for 3D-Printed Microfluidics

2611.23915.abstract: The surface Cahn--Hilliard equation describes phase separation and coarsening of a conserved composition field on fixed curved surfaces. We study a mixed $hp$-surface finite element discretization with curvilinear high-order elements, primarily on the sphere, with the stabilized semi-implicit BDF2 integrator and a stabilized convex-splitting variant solved with the same factorization. For the semi-implicit scheme with a quadratic-growth potential and a truncated nonlinear bulk chemical-potential term, we prove exact discrete mass conservation, energy decay for the start-up steps, an exact per-step energy balance for the BDF2 phase, and a conditional monotone law for a modified Lyapunov functional. A manufactured solution with analytic forcing verifies second order in time and the expected $h$- and $p$-convergence. Torus tests include controlled equal-area bands, whose diffuse energies reproduce sharp-interface perimeters within $1\%$, deterministic coarsening, and a viscous R{ä}tz--Voigt model. Genus-two and genus-three calculations on implicit surfaces conserve mass to roundoff, and their unstable-mode counts agree with area-based Weyl estimates within $1\%$.
2611.23915.title: Semi-Implicit and Convex Splitting Schemes for the Surface Cahn--Hilliard Equation on Curved Closed Surfaces

2611.23981.abstract: We consider the partition sum $Z_L(t)$ of two non-crossing continuum directed polymers of length $t$, in a common random medium with the geometry of a cylinder of circumference length $L$. In the limit $t \to +\infty$, the $k$-th cumulant of (minus) the free energy $\log Z_L(t)$, grows as $c_k(L) t$, and we compute the amplitudes $c_k(L)$. To this aim we first study the integer moments $\langle Z_L(t)^n \rangle$, whose long-time behavior is determined by the ground-state energy of the one-dimensional attractive Lieb--Liniger model in the symmetry sector associated with the Young diagram $(n,n)$ (a two-component bosonic nested Bethe ansatz). This ground state energy is obtained using the nested Bethe-Ansatz involving $2n$ physical rapidities and $n$ auxiliary rapidities. The analytic continuation in the replica number $n$, which yields the cumulants $c_k(L)$, is performed through a non-trivial generalization of the method developed by Brunet and Derrida for a single polymer on the cylinder. We obtain fully explicit formulas for the mean $c_1(L)$ and the variance $c_2(L)$, and construct a systematic scheme for computing all higher cumulants $c_k(L)$. Finally, taking $L\to+\infty$ and $n\to0$ with $nL^{1/2}$ fixed, we derive a universal scaling function which characterizes the large-deviation statistics of the two-polymer free energy and is expected to be universal within the one-dimensional two-layer periodic SHE/KPZ class. The two tails of the large-deviation function are obtained analytically, revealing different roles of the non-crossing constraint in favorable and unfavorable fluctuations of the common disorder.
2611.23981.title: Free energy distribution for two non-crossing directed polymers on the cylinder

2611.24008.abstract: The human-exoskeleton interaction interface, consisting of the exoskeleton attachment and the underlying human soft tissue, can affect the transfer of assistance. MuJoCo's \textit{flexcomp} has been previously used to model the soft tissue, but its accuracy has not been benchmarked against a finite element model. We benchmarked the \textit{flexcomp} Saint Venant-Kirchhoff (StVK) and Stable Neo-Hookean (SNH) models against COMSOL's Yeoh model in three cases: \textit{case 1}) spherical indentation, \textit{case 2}) compression, and \textit{case 3}) compression of a thigh. We compared force and strain energy as a function of indentation depth, hysteresis and computation time. MuJoCo's models capture force trends with a correlation of 0.97-0.99, but showed a stiffer response, which could be attributed to the volumetric locking of the linear finite elements. The MuJoCo models systematically underestimated hysteresis as MuJoCo's Rayleigh damping could not substitute a viscoelastic model. Moreover, MuJoCo's computational advantage was speed dependent: it was 2-2.5 times faster for spherical indentation, but COMSOL was faster for the other cases, which have more degrees of freedom and contacts. Although MuJoCo's \textit{flexcomp} offers a combination of soft-tissue modelling and multibody dynamics, the limitations regarding the stiffening and hysteresis should be addressed to be used for the analysis of the human-exoskeleton interaction interface.
2611.24008.title: Modelling the human-exoskeleton interaction interface - Benchmarking MuJoCo's deformable model

2611.24141.abstract: Type-A Portevin--Le Chatelier bands are propagating strain localizations whose velocity exhibits strong intermittent fluctuations. We derive a coarse-grained connection between the dynamic-strain-aging model of Hähner and Rizzi and the Alessandro--Beatrice--Bertotti--Montorsi (ABBM) mean-field model of avalanche dynamics. A propagating band is reduced to a single phase coordinate while retaining the elastic feedback of the tensile machine. This feedback generates the increasing drive and restoring terms of the ABBM description. A finite-time adjoint calculation determines the stress mobility of the band and is checked independently by direct stress continuation. The mobility is approximately proportional to the hardening parameter, whereas the band speed scales approximately as its square root. Short-range heterogeneity in the plastic strain deposited by the band is converted by the global machine feedback into a Brownian effective force. The resulting reduction provides a microscopic route from dynamic strain aging to ABBM-like avalanche dynamics of propagating PLC bands.
2611.24141.title: From dynamic strain aging to Alessandro--Beatrice--Bertotti--Montorsi dynamics of propagating Portevin--Le Chatelier bands

2611.24369.abstract: Time-bin entanglement is promising for satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) due to its compatibility with telecom fiber networks, but its phase-sensitive measurements are vulnerable to Doppler effects induced by satellite motion. We present a spectral-temporal framework for time-bin-entangled photon pairs generated onboard a satellite via Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) and distributed to two Optical Ground Stations (OGSs) over independent downlinks with distinct Doppler shifts. Each OGS is equipped with an Unbalanced Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (UMZI) used to perform Bennett-Brassard-Mermin 1992 (BBM92) entangled-photon QKD. In a simulated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) pass with matched 400 ps analyzer delays, the received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by about 38 rad, which primarily degrades phase-basis correlations. After zero-Doppler calibration, this phase separates into independent signal-and idler-link contributions, allowing each station to correct its link Doppler phase shift locally, without real-time phase exchange between the stations. We propose an ephemeris-assisted feed-forward architecture, in which an auxiliary interferometer analyzes a co-propagating classical witness field to reconstruct the local Doppler-induced phase, which a phase modulator then compensates on the quantum channel. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction rate keeps the phase-basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) below 2% and retains 93% of the ideal asymptotic key yield. After 18 accumulated passes, the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, whereas relabeling the parity from the ephemeris without optical correction reaches only about 8%.
2611.24369.title: Doppler effect on dual-downlink time-bin quantum key distribution and a proposed ephemeris-assisted witness-field correction

2611.24391.abstract: The microscopic mechanisms of heat transport in structurally disordered polymer-carbon composites remain incompletely understood, particularly over the broad temperature range extending from cryogenic to ambient conditions. Here, we investigate the relationship between structural organization and thermal transport in epoxy-graphene oxide (GO) composites with nominal GO contents of 0.25-10 wt.% relative to the resin (0.21-6.1 wt.% of the total composite mass). X-ray diffraction reveals predominantly amorphous scattering without a detectable GO(001) reflection, suggesting substantial suppression of ordered GO stacking within the cured epoxy matrix. Raman spectroscopy confirms the increasing contribution of the carbon phase while revealing no pronounced changes in the characteristic vibrational bands of the epoxy network. Thermal-conductivity measurements (4.5-300 K) demonstrate that GO incorporation modifies the temperature dependence of heat transport rather than producing a simple conductivity enhancement. The experimental data are described by a phenomenological multichannel model comprising a temperature-independent plateau term and two or three effective Arrhenius-type contributions characterized by distinct temperature scales ranging from a few to several hundred kelvin. The low-temperature conductivity plateau observed at lower GO concentrations is no longer resolved in GO-6 and GO-10, indicating a qualitative change in the temperature dependence of heat transport. These results establish a correlation between structural organization and the redistribution of effective thermal-transport contributions in epoxy-GO composites, providing an experimental basis for further microscopic interpretation within the framework of unified vibrational thermal-transport theory.

2611.24391.title: Structure and Thermal Conductivity of Epoxy-Graphene Oxide Composites from 4.5 to 300 K

2611.24414.abstract: In heterogeneous materials, surface roughness, chemical incompatibility, mechanical mismatch or manufacturing defects result in imperfect bonding between the constituents. Such imperfections introduce a finite-thickness interphase zone between the constituents that possess a graded or inhomogeneous micro-structure. It is virtually impossible to resolve the behavior of such interphases. Instead, a well-established approach is to replace the interphase by a zero-thickness interface endowed with its own energetic structure. Conventional interface models define the interface temperature as an average of the temperatures of the surrounding bulk phases. However, this assumption is only adequate to represent uniform homogeneous interphases and it fails to accurately capture the behavior of graded or inhomogeneous interphases. In this work, we address this limitation by allowing for unequal contributions of the surrounding bulk phases to the interface temperature. We systematically revisit the resulting balance equations and present the computational framework for the finite element implementation of the model. We further incorporate the proposed model within the homogenization framework and derive closed-form analytical expressions for the effective thermal conductivity of fiber- and particle-reinforced composites, accouting for the influence of the extended general interface. Finally, through a series of numerical examples, we demonstrate the capabilities of the proposed model and investigate the influence of its parameters on the size-dependent thermal behavior of composites.
2611.24414.title: On the thermal behavior of composites embedding extended general interfaces

2611.25176.abstract: The number of large loads connected to the bulk power system has been increasing rapidly worldwide. Emerging high-demand facilities, particularly AI data centers, are introducing new challenges for power system planners. In absence of appropriate planning mechanisms, the addition of high volumes of data center loads will lead to an increase in outages, thus degrading reliability of the system. Energy storage systems (ESS) offer a promising solution to mitigate the reliability impacts of these large loads, due to their flexibility and fast-ramping characteristics. However, ESS should be judiciously sized and sited to maximize the reliability benefits to the grid. This paper presents a framework for the optimal sizing and siting of ESS to minimize the adverse reliability impacts of large load additions. First, a stochastic semi-Markov model is developed to model the load of AI data centers and generate profiles for several such facilities. These profiles are then incorporated into a Markov-chain Monte Carlo simulation-based composite system reliability assessment framework. A detailed nodal network model is used to quantify the reliability impacts of adding data centers and to identify buses most affected by large loads. Resource adequacy metrics are used to evaluate the overall system reliability impacts. ESS are then strategically sized and sited based on this analysis to mitigate the negative impacts of large loads on overall system reliability. The proposed framework is demonstrated using the RTS-GMLC 72-bus test system. The results show how ESS can effectively enhance system reliability in the presence of rapidly growing large-load demand. This framework provides system planners, utilities, and regulators with a practical tool for maintaining reliable power system operation using energy storage as more large loads are integrated into the grid.
2611.25176.comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, published as part of the proceedings of the 2026 Grid of the Future Symposium organized by the CIGRE US National Committee
2611.25176.title: Reliability-based Sizing of Energy Storage for Large Load Integration

2611.25528.abstract: Branched macromolecular architectures are ubiquitous in living systems and synthetic polymeric systems, create topologically complex media that strongly influence tracer dynamics beyond simple packing fraction-driven crowding effects. Motivated by biological systems such as amoebae, astrocytes, cytoskeletal assemblies, and cyclic bottlebrushes, we investigate active and passive tracer transport in polymeric environments of topologically distinct architectures. Here, using Langevin dynamics simulations, we focus on how polymer topology alters diffusion behavior in a branched-ring polymeric (BRP) environment. To isolate the role of intramolecular topology from monomer density, we specifically benchmark the BRP dynamics against an unlinked linear-ring polymer mixture (LRM). In general, we find that while passive tracers are largely unaffected by the polymer connectivity and bending rigidity, the self-propelled active tracers strongly distinguish between the two architectures. Increasing chain rigidity facilitates active diffusion in the unlinked LRM but strongly restricts mobility in the BRP matrix, driving a transition to pronounced long-time subdiffusion that becomes more prominent with propulsion strength. Different physical observables reveal that interconnected topological cages are formed in the stiff limit, leading to transient weak ergodicity breaking and leptokurtic displacement statistics. Further, the self-intermediate scattering function confirms that the short-range dynamics remain unaltered by the matrix connectivity, while relaxation at large spatial length scales is governed by the topological caging. Finally, varying the branch length and number, we identified an optimal branch architecture that maximizes active trapping. Our results establish that macromolecular connectivity and stiffness dominate the active transport even in the system of identical packing fraction.
2611.25528.title: Topological trapping of active tracers in branched ring polymer matrices

2611.25779.abstract: The ability to measure thermal properties and visualize heat transport processes with high spatial resolution is becoming increasingly important for materials discovery, next-generation electronics, and advanced manufacturing. As critical dimensions and architectures of novel materials and high performance electronics shrink and become more heterogeneous, thermal transport is no longer governed by bulk material properties alone, but by local variations in microstructure, such as interfaces and defects, while the operating conditions can also play a role. With the development of non-contact pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques, specific heat, thermal conductivity, and interface conductance can be mapped either through wide-field thermos-reflectance images or by scanning technique. However, key challenges remain such as the balance between imaging throughput and measurement accuracy, the extraction of multiple parameters with high confidence, and non-intrusive subsurface characterization, etc. This Review highlights recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI)-assistance in high-throughput data processing, visualizing interfacial thermal transport, and nonintrusive subsurface analysis, and offers outlooks for future research directions such as spectral mapping of heat carriers, three-dimensional property mapping, and AI-agentic experimental designs. We anticipate this Review will motivate future efforts in combining AI with experimental techniques to achieve unprecedented capabilities for thermal characterization of nanoscale materials and device characterization, facilitating materials discovery and electronics revolution.
2611.25779.title: Intelligent Imaging of Thermal Transport in Nanostructures

2611.25991.abstract: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts are highly sensitive to the fiber-orientation field supplied to the material model. In conventional workflows, that field comes from resin-flow analysis, which requires molding-specialist support and takes about 25 hours of work per part. We previously proposed a surrogate model that addresses this bottleneck by predicting the orientation field in about 3 minutes. This paper reports the implementation, validation, and operational design that turned the model into an engineering tool for Honda design workflows. We present staged validation from 2D plates to production parts, evaluation against a predefined engineering angular-error criterion, and the expert review that approved design use in March 2025; the system has since been transferred to the crash-safety group and is in initial, limited use in directed fracture-prediction scenarios. The developed system combines injection-gate setting support for cases in which gates are unknown (90% gate-count accuracy, mean position error 11% of flow length), voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and report generation in a single GUI. The complete orientation-preparation workflow takes about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the conventional 25-hour flow-analysis route, and can be run directly by crash CAE engineers without molding-specialist support. As evidence of practical impact, component-level crash analysis using the predicted orientation field reduced the absolute peak-force error from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%, while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region. The deployment lesson is that a surrogate model alone is not enough for practical adoption: gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and shareable reporting are what make the model usable as a design tool.
2611.25991.comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IAAI-27 (AAAI 2027), with technical appendices. 10 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables
2611.25991.title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE

2611.26128.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) determines macromolecular structures from noisy particle images. However, rare, transient compositional states and subtle, continuous conformational variation are difficult to resolve. We present CryoGaussian, a Gaussian splatting method for heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction that fits an explicit Gaussian density representation directly to the particle images through a differentiable rasterizer rendering orthographic line integrals modulated by the contrast transfer function. The Gaussians are initialized randomly, with their number derived from the estimated spatial support of the molecular density and their minimum size bounded by the Nyquist frequency of the particle images. To capture the compositional and conformational variation across particle images, we learn particle-image and per-Gaussian latents that jointly modulate the base position, amplitude, and scale of each Gaussian. Each structural state is then reconstructed by fitting the Gaussians conditioned on its inferred latent. On CryoBench, CryoGaussian achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy for both compositional and conformational heterogeneity. On experimental data, it resolves a rare compositional state of the 50S ribosomal subunit (class C4, 1.3% of particles) with rRNA helix 68 docked in the absence of the central protuberance, and continuous conformational motion of the SF3b and helicase subcomplexes of the pre-catalytic spliceosome. We further optimize the rasterizer for additive cryo-EM projection, reducing training time by 12.8-28.0$\times$.
2611.26128.title: CryoGaussian: Heterogeneous Cryo-EM Reconstruction Made Explicit with Gaussian Splatting

2611.26236.abstract: Stirring and shear usually suppress phase separation, but transport through a boundary can induce it. We study a binary mixture that is stable everywhere at rest and fills a two-dimensional annulus. The inner boundary is semipermeable and exchanges material with a permeate held at a fixed chemical potential, so that a steady flux of one component crosses the annulus. Although this driven system carries a steady current and produces entropy, within Model B dynamics its steady state is an equilibrium profile in an effective external field that is logarithmic in the distance from the center. Its strength is not imposed from outside but set by the permeate and the permeability of the boundary. Above a threshold driving flux, a condensed annulus forms around the inner boundary. It is bounded by a stationary front whose radius depends exponentially on the ratio of the bulk driving force to the flux. The front is pinned by the effective field and does not coarsen, and the threshold flux decreases only as the inverse logarithm of the system size. The driving flux shifts the phase lines but leaves the critical temperature unchanged. Interfacial tension gives rise to a critical nucleus and to a fold, at which the condensed state ceases to exist, with a threshold that we obtain in closed form. Numerical solutions confirm these predictions and reveal a hysteresis loop bounded by two saddle-node bifurcations. By symmetry, the theory also describes cavitation around a sink.
2611.26236.title: Flux-induced condensation in a radial geometry

2611.26892.abstract: Helical polypeptides combine the chemical tunability of synthetic macromolecules with the highly ordered backbone architecture of natural proteins. Here, density-functional tight-binding calculations are used to determine how chain length and sequence chemistry govern the dipolar and electronic properties of three $α$-helical polypeptide families: polyalanine [AAAAA]$_n$, leucine-modified [AAAAL]$_n$, and cysteine-capped, lysine-containing C[AAAAK]$_n$. Increasing chain length produces systematic shifts and splitting of the molecular orbital levels together with an approximately additive increase in the molecular dipole. Analysis of the C[AAAAK]$_3$ helix shows that aligned backbone carbonyl groups provide the dominant contribution to the macro dipole, whose growing electrostatic potential is consistent with an intrinsic Stark-like contribution to the length-dependent orbital-energy evolution. Side-chain and terminal modifications introduce localized perturbations to frontier electronic states while preserving this global backbone-driven trend. Residue-resolved frontier levels additionally form a staircase-like energy landscape along the helical scaffold: individual peptide units retain large local HOMO-LUMO gaps of approximately 5 eV, whereas spatially proximate hydrogen-bonded residues exhibit smaller inter-residue energy separations. Application of external electrostatic fields modifies the frontier-level separation in a direction-dependent manner and induces structural distortions predominantly near the flexible termini, while the helical core remains comparatively robust. By establishing these fundamental sequence-structure-property relationships, this work provides a foundational blueprint for the rational design of peptide-based biomacromolecules tailored for next-generation bio-electronic interfaces, biosensors, and artificial electron-transfer systems.
2611.26892.comment: Manuscript: 19 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables; SI: 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 table
2611.26892.title: Length and Sequence-Dependent Dipolar and Electronic Properties of $α$-helical Polypeptides

2611.27259.abstract: Nanoparticle-induced local interface regions significantly enhance the bulk mechanical behavior of polymer nanocomposites, yet their energetic contribution in crosslinked elastomer networks remains poorly understood. Here, we decouple the entropic and enthalpic contributions to the elasticity of crosslinked poly(dimethylsiloxane) nanocomposites using temperature-dependent thermomechanical measurements. While the measured bulk elastic modulus exhibits a monotonic increase with nanoparticle volume fraction $φ_{\rm n}$, we observe that the effective crosslink density initially increases before saturating at larger $φ_{\rm n}$. These results are independently validated across two nanoparticle systems (silica and titania) and directly confirmed by X-ray scattering experiments on silica-based composites, highlighting the generality of the observation. The trends in effective crosslink density indicate that the elastic response is predominantly entropy-driven at low nanoparticle concentrations, whereas enthalpic contributions become increasingly significant at higher loadings. Assuming a linear superposition of interface and bulk contributions, these results reveal that the effective crosslink density at the particle interface decreases by an order of magnitude below a critical mean interparticle separation, indicating that localized particle proximity and clustering constrain the entropic elasticity at higher loadings.
2611.27259.title: Decoupling Entropic and Enthalpic Elasticity in Crosslinked Polymer Nanocomposites

2611.27292.abstract: Although mathematical modeling and numerical simulations for two-phase Newtonian flows have been extensively studied for many years, relatively little work has focused on developing thermodynamically consistent models for two-phase Non-Newtonian viscoelastic flows, and to the author's best konowledge, no structure-preserving numerical methods have been reported for such models. In this paper, we focus on modeling the two-phase non-Newtonnian visco-elastic FENE-P model based on the energetic variational approach (EnVarA). In the model, a phase-field function is introduced to describe the diffuse interface which satisfies the Cahn-Hilliard (CH) equation. And all the physical variables can be connected smoothly. We conduct a matched asymptotic analysis for the sharp interface limit, which shows the diffuse interface model will converge to the sharp interface model when the interface thickness trends to zero. We then reformulate the model in an equivalent form that facilitates the construction of the numerical scheme. A weakly decoupled scheme is proposed for the resulting FENE-P-CH system, and its unconditional energy stability is proved theoretically. Finally, a series of numerical experiments is conducted to validate the model and assess the performance of the proposed scheme.
2611.27292.title: Two-phase visco-elastic FENE-P model: Thermodynamically consistent modeling, sharp interface limit analysis and unconditionally energy stable numerical scheme

2611.27480.abstract: Balancing high performance with sustainability in microelectronics is challenged by energy-intensive processes, scarce materials and limited recyclability. Inspired by nature, a promising solution relies on the evolution of the foundry model to transient microelectronics, using electrochemistry to grow adaptive circuits on demand and during operation. To this end, this study explores how to harness the morphogenesis of conducting polymer dendrites between stacks of micro-electrode arrays to dynamically interconnect them with voltage pulses. Using propylene carbonate as a solvent, we investigated the dynamics of the electroconvective growth of poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT), revealing strong structural dependencies between the morphology of the electrogenerated polymer and the confinement of the micro-electrodes. As the system evolves from 2D flat patterns to 3D dendritic structures, the capability of the conducting polymer to locally interconnect specific nodes heavily depends on the size and density of the arrays which directly impact the flow distribution during growth. By unraveling how a device geometry enables the growth of dendritic interconnections on integrated micro-electrode arrays, the morphogenesis of conducting polymer dendrites not only addresses the longstanding issue of heterogeneous integration in microelectronics, but also opens the way to a paradigm where electronic devices learn as they grow in our pockets.
2611.27480.title: Sprouting Fields of Conducting Polymer Dendrites as Evolving Organic Electrochemical Frameworks to Interconnect Electrode Arrays

2611.27581.abstract: The interplay between quenched disorder and collective interactions can generate multiple emergent lengthscales in damage processes, yet their roles in determining the strength of heterogeneous materials remain incompletely understood. Here, we develop a coarse-grained description of load redistribution in the two-dimensional random fuse model (RFM) with Weibull-distributed quenched disorder, interpreting shielding in the crack-tip damage density as a consequence of nonlocal current redistribution. Our numerical results distinguish this emergent screening length, identified as the size of the statistical fracture process zone, from the regularizing length in Bazant's established quasibrittle size-effect law (SEL), revealing their distinct disorder dependences, and challenging previous associations of the two. We further uncover a comparable scaling between the SEL and pre-failure crack extension, suggesting the former may instead be more naturally associated with a percolation process of micro-fractures around the crack-tip. These findings disentangle important emergent lengthscales within the RFM, and highlight a candidate physical mechanism for explaining macroscopic size effects in quasibrittle fracture.
2611.27581.title: Disentangling Lengthscales in Disordered Fracture

2611.27636.abstract: The development of advanced detector technologies will play a key role in future high-energy physics experiments, such as the FCC-ee. In this context, chromatic calorimetry is an emerging concept for electromagnetic calorimeters, with the potential to combine the precise energy measurement of homogeneous calorimeters with longitudinal reconstruction of particle showers. The state of the art in chromatic calorimetry is reviewed, including experimental results from proof-of-concept prototypes and simulation studies investigating quantum-dot-based configurations. Recent progress and current challenges in the development of nanocomposites are also discussed. Finally, future prospects for chromatic calorimetry are outlined.
2611.27636.comment: Contribution to the 43rd International Conference on High Energy Physics (ICHEP 2026)
2611.27636.title: Chromatic calorimetry using nanocomposites: status and future challenges

2611.27644.abstract: This study investigates the transient swelling of an initially spherical magnetoelastic hydrogel balloon. The balloon is inflated at constant internal pressure and exposed to the non-uniform magnetic field of one or two current-carrying coils. The gel is modelled as a compressible Ogden network mixed with solvent through Flory--Huggins theory, with an additive elastic--mixing--magnetic decomposition of the free energy. A fully coupled nonlinear finite element formulation uses a staggered solution scheme and a Taylor--Hood-type discretisation. It follows the balloon from its dry inflated state to either swollen equilibrium or burst. The formulation recovers the analytical free-swelling stretch and the delayed-burst regime, and its converged states agree with equilibrium energy minimisation. Symmetry-breaking (pear-shaped) dry configurations do not survive swelling: they rearrange rapidly and then relax by diffusion onto the symmetric branch. Transient membrane stresses can exceed their equilibrium values by nearly an order of magnitude. For coils which are sufficiently close to undeformed balloon, fields beyond a critical intensity close the slow-inflation curve into a loop. Stable swollen equilibria then exist only within a bounded pressure window that narrows as the field increases, and outside of it the balloon bursts. Under two coaxial coils, asymmetry about the equator appears only when the coils differ in current or radius. The magnetic field therefore acts as a control parameter for shape of balloon and permits or prevents stable swelling at a given pressure.
2611.27644.title: A nonlinear transient finite element analysis of coupled solvent diffusion and large deformation of magneto-elastic hydrogel balloon

2611.27846.abstract: We study the average excess pseudo entropy, $ΔS_{12}$, in the Rice-Mele model under Thouless pumping. We compute it for two driving schemes, the control-freak and smooth pumps, under open and periodic boundary conditions. We find that $ΔS_{12}$ distinguishes the trivial, monomer, and topological stages of the pump, and that it depends on the boundary condition, the driving scheme, and the reference time. We also find that a nonzero staggered potential breaks chiral symmetry and gaps out the SSH critical point, thereby flattening the pseudo-entropy peak at the phase boundary. We also study reference-state dependence in the open Kitaev chain, comparing a fixed even-parity target with five reference families: even free-fermion, pairing-only, vacuum, and two fixed gapped states. We find that the pseudo-entropy response depends on the reference and on the parity of the subsystem size, even when the reference remains gapped. At $μ=0$, the pairing-only reference gives the exact result $S_{\mathrm{pr}}=\ln 2$ for $L=4m+2$, while the $L=4m$ sequence has analytically determined finite-size corrections. These results show that, in both models, pseudo entropy is a property of the reference-target pair and the subsystem partition, rather than a reference-independent signature of the topological phase.
2611.27846.title: Pseudo-entropy in Thouless Pumps and Majorana Topological Phases

2611.27923.abstract: Public authorities increasingly need to translate multifaceted policy objectives into concrete fiscal and investment choices while accounting for their socioeconomic consequences. A credible ex-ante impact assessment should report downstream implications attributable to the historical baseline and specified policy targets, without introducing discretionary assumptions about unknown administrative, socioeconomic or other physical processes. Bringing the large-scale perspective of statistical physics to public governance, we construct such an ex-ante impact assessment. Its scope encompasses policy objectives that condition a finite number of generalized moments of observables in the historical baseline, which comprises a sufficiently large collection of projects or public programmes. As a proof-of-principle application, we consider the green transition in the energy-generation sector using the historical baseline of many infrastructure projects from the World Bank. Our earlier results deriving closed-form expressions for coarse-grained combinatorial probabilities enable a tractable statistical and downstream assessment. We assess the statistical compatibility of the historical baseline with different levels of green-power surplus and demonstrate how the same statistical-physics construction can estimate any downstream metric expressible through arbitrary functions of generalized moments of the baseline observables. In the absence of more detailed knowledge about the processes forming the historical baseline, large-scale universality, whenever many unknown influences on collective phenomena become negligible, unambiguously offers a principled route to a self-contained ex-ante impact assessment.
2611.27923.title: The Fiscal and Economic Implications of Green Mandates: a Boltzmann Approach to Public Governance

2611.28322.abstract: A viscoelastic framework is developed through a moment reduction of the hereditary integral defining the free energy of transient polymer networks. Expanding the chain energy about the mean history invariant produces a hierarchy of tensorial moments representing the network formation history. For energies depending on the relative first invariant, the leading approximation recovers Lubliner's model, providing a physical interpretation of its second-rank history tensor as an average of the inverse deformation metrics at chain formation. The next approximation introduces a fourth-rank tensor that accounts for variability among formation configurations. These moments admit equivalent rate forms and efficient recurrence relations, while their evolution permits the establishment of sufficient conditions for dissipation. Comparisons with an exact hereditary representation of the three-term Arruda-Boyce energy demonstrate that the first-moment approximation captures the overall response, while retaining the second moment improves accuracy, particularly under complex loading histories. We also incorporate non-exponential relaxation through distributed detachment kinetics described by the Kohlrausch-Williams-Watts (KWW) function. Assuming thermorheological simplicity, calibration to thermally accelerated butyl-rubber relaxation measurements yields excellent agreement across wide ranges of time and temperature. The calibrated continuous rate spectrum is then discretized into a finite Prony series using equal-probability bins. The proposed framework provides a practical representation of nonlinear transient network behavior that separates the approximation of deformation history from the discretization of the continuous rate spectrum.
2611.28322.title: Moment-Based Transient Network Models for Finite-Strain Viscoelasticity

2611.28772.abstract: Multi-axis, multi-material additive manufacturing enables the production of conformal electronic systems that are difficult to realise using planar processes and can offer enhanced performance; however, accessibility and reproducibility remain challenging. This paper presents MM-Open5x, an open and low-cost multi-material, multi-axis additive manufacturing workflow for practical conformal electronics. The workflow spans design, simulation, toolpath generation, fabrication, testing, and assembly, and is released alongside complete design files, toolpaths, and representative G-code. Representative case studies demonstrate both the benefits and limitations of multi-axis deposition in practice, explicitly documenting common failure modes, calibration sensitivities, assembly bottlenecks, and material variability. Rather than prescribing an optimal solution, MM-Open5x is presented as a transparent, reproducible foundation upon which a broader community can iterate, extend, and apply conformal electronics workflows across diverse application domains.
2611.28772.comment: 4 pages, 5 figures, To appear in the Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Additively Manufactured Electronic Systems (AMES) 2026
2611.28772.title: MM-Open5x: Practical Conformal Electronics via Multi-Material Multi-Axis Additive Manufacturing

2611.28961.abstract: Time-resolved crystallography (TRX) captures macromolecules in action, but a triggered crystal contains a mixture of triggered proteins in an unknown state and untriggered proteins in the reference state. Separating these is necessary to isolate the dynamics of interest and is an underdetermined data-analysis task. For the simplest case, with one triggered state and one reference state, a range of methods exists, but their assumptions, accuracy, and domains of applicability have not been systematically investigated. Here, we deconstruct and review the methods in current use, employing a unified notation. We make their assumptions explicit and benchmark each on a simulated dataset. A key point is that many of these methods do not estimate the fraction of all triggered molecules in the crystal, but instead estimate a latent parameter we call the extrapolation factor, which is related to but distinct from the so-called "occupancy". As our simulations make apparent, current methods do not always yield accurate results, in particular with noisy data and when the fraction of triggered protein is low. Inspired by previous work, we introduce Vacuum Level Matching, a method that grounds the estimate in the physical constraint that electron density is a nonnegative quantity: it cannot fall below a vacuum level. Operating voxel by voxel, Vacuum Level Matching replaces the manual choices of previous methods with a data-driven procedure and reports quality-control metrics that flag data unable to support a confident prediction. On the same simulated data, it outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and on two experimental datasets, rsEGFP2 and a multi-time-point photolyase series, it recovers known structural changes while flagging issues where the data are weak. Finally, we report an implementation of Vacuum Level Matching in the form of a small, reusable Python package.
2611.28961.title: Estimating Extrapolation Factors in Time-Resolved Crystallography

2611.29010.abstract: Two-photon lithography (TPL) prints three-dimensional polymer architectures with sub-diffraction features, but writing them voxel by voxel limits its throughput. This review examines how parallelization overcomes this limit with fixed multi-focus arrays, reconfigurable holography using spatial light modulators and digital micromirror devices, hybrid metalens arrays, shaped beams, temporally focused projection and two-step absorption. An energy-deposition framework built on measured nonlinear absorption coefficients shows how the absorption order and coefficients of a resist determine its voxel size, energy per voxel and attainable voxel rate. Applied to parallel writing, the framework quantifies the costs of non-uniform foci, coherent crosstalk between foci, side-lobe losses in shaped beams and weaker axial confinement in projection. Published systems reach peak rates above $10^{8}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with scanned focus arrays and up to $1.7\times10^{9}$ voxels s$^{-1}$ with grayscale projection under a fine-voxel definition, and parallel features as small as 20-55 nm. As rates rise, however, dose uniformity, proximity effects, heat, stitching and data bandwidth increasingly limit fidelity. A minimum reporting standard that includes the energy per voxel and sustained part-level rates is therefore proposed, together with priorities for the field: shared benchmark parts, predictive dose control and resists designed for parallel writing.
2611.29010.title: Parallel Two-Photon Lithography: From Optical Nonlinearities to Energy Limits, Dose Control and Throughput Benchmarks

2611.29649.abstract: Even under identical external conditions, a driven system can occupy distinct long-lived states with different susceptibilities to the same rare transition. We demonstrate this in a confined partially active polymer, where independent unknotted replicas occupy distinct mechanical states with different topological futures. Matched-control and event-resolved analyses reveal a susceptible reservoir and a short threading precursor. We test this state dependence prospectively by launching 2272 Langevin-noise branches from 71 preserved unknotted phase-space states using a classifier prespecified from independent data. Most strikingly, the same classifier strongly separates finite-time knotting at one pore radius, yet reverses its susceptibility ordering at a neighboring radius. Thus geometry does not merely shift an average knotting rate; it selects among long-lived nonequilibrium states and reorganizes the mapping between a pre-existing mechanical coordinate and future topological fate.
2611.29649.title: Geometry Reorganizes Nonequilibrium States that Gate Topological Switching in an Active Polymer

2611.30058.abstract: Field-mediated forces between particles can be both nonreciprocal and irreducibly multi-body, giving rise to emergent activity in systems of individually passive particles. While prior work extensively studied how multi-body nonreciprocity can activate few-body systems, fuel intermittency, and drive liquid-like behavior, the effect on the solid state of large particle ensembles is less explored. Here we use two-dimensional, close-packed rafts of identical, athermal, acoustically levitated microspheres to show how multi-body nonreciprocity injects activity in solids. At the level of both individual particles and collective dynamics, crystalline rafts exhibit persistent circulations with no net handedness. The rafts also exhibit a phonon-like dispersion relation corresponding to a large Poisson ratio, indicating an induced softness to shear. Within the bulk, lattice symmetry masks microscopic nonreciprocity, although it can manifest in renormalized, reciprocal elastic coefficients. At dislocations and raft edges, where this symmetry is broken, multi-body nonreciprocal interactions act as local generators of activity. A coarse-grained microscopic model of multi-body nonreciprocity, calibrated on three-particle simulations, recovers the rafts' experimentally observed dispersion relations and localized activity. Using these findings, we illustrate how to harness defect-induced activity for programmable movement by arranging microscopic dislocations to drive macroscopic propulsion and rotation of a whole raft.
2611.30058.title: Solids activated by multi-body nonreciprocity

2611.30660.abstract: We derive and analyze a phase-field model describing the formation of the active layer of organic solar cells. The process combines phase separation of an electron donor (polymer) and an electron acceptor (non-fullerene acceptor) with evaporation of a solvent. Taking the macroscopic motion of the fluid into account, this results in a coupled system of incompressible Navier--Stokes, degenerate multispecies Cahn--Hilliard, and Allen--Cahn equations with cross-diffusion terms. We give a thermodynamically consistent derivation of the system and prove the existence of global-in-time weak solutions without any size constraints on the data. The solutions dissipate the total energy and require an ad-hoc variational formulation of the definition of the diffusion fluxes, which is made necessary by the degeneracy of the mobility matrix.
2611.30660.title: Modeling and analysis of a phase-field model for organic solar cells

2611.30794.abstract: We present a theoretical framework for predicting pulse-to-pulse power fluctuations caused by pump and seed power noise and by amplified spontaneous emission in ultrafast fiber amplifiers operating in the gain-managed nonlinear regime. The numerical model evaluates statistically averaged quantities directly, without Monte Carlo simulations with stochastic sources, and reduces to a semi-analytical monochromatic model in the limit of vanishing signal bandwidth and negligible ASE. We show that nonlinear spectral broadening of the signal and of its perturbations, combined with the frequency-dependent gain, significantly alters the technical relative intensity noise in both the high-power, high-repetition-rate and the low-power, low-repetition-rate regimes, and that in the latter regime the contributions related to amplified spontaneous emission become comparable to those induced by pump and seed fluctuations.
2611.30794.title: Pulse-to-pulse Power Fluctuations in Ultra-Fast Fiber Amplifiers with Gain-Managed Nonlinearity

2611.30910.abstract: Active systems and other coarse-grained descriptions are often modeled by generalized dynamics, effective equations of motion that are not bound by the constraints of genuinely microscopic physics. In particular, these equations are generally stochastic on the smallest resolved scale. This poses a challenge to first-principles statistical physics, which usually derives emergent noise on larger scales from deterministic interactions. Here, we show how to systematically incorporate microscopic noise into kinetic theory in the limit of weak noise, i.e., high activity. By means of a Dyson expansion of the noisy free propagator, we derive the leading correction to the Landau kinetic equation for weakly interacting systems. We find that the common practice of combining a deterministic collision integral with the diffusive terms of the Fokker--Planck equation is the correct leading order. For dry aligning active matter, however, the corrections are non-analytic in the noise strength, as nearly parallel particles interact for arbitrarily long times. For noise that acts only during interactions, a minimal model of stochastic interactions, noise and collisions do not decouple: the leading corrections are odd in the coupling strength, partly logarithmically enhanced, and amount to an orientation-dependent effective noise strength. Agent-based simulations confirm the predicted dependence on the sign of the coupling. Even in this minimal model, the effect of noise on collisions can thus not be inferred from symmetry alone.
2611.30910.title: Statistical mechanics of noisy collisions in active matter: Dyson-Landau theory

2611.31325.abstract: Recently, in the 1D Takayasu Mass Model (MM) of diffusion-aggregation with input, large condensates and a novel power law were observed in simulations, and later characterised exactly. We extend these studies to the Takayasu model with generalised input, and provide a relation to translate the distribution function of the MM to any model with a space and time independent injection process. In the 1D Charge Model (CM) of a system of size $L$, where $q=+1$ and $-1$ charge monomers are injected with equal probability at each site in each time step, there is a power law distribution of cluster charge $P(q)\sim |q|^{-5/3}$. This distribution cuts off at $|q|\sim L^{3/2}$ in the steady state for long times $t\gg L^2$ and a large charge condensate forms with a net charge between $-\sqrt{Lt}$ and $\sqrt{Lt}$. A distance dependent distribution function is observed around the charge condensate and near open boundaries, both of which act like an edge in the system, analogous to the observations in the MM. The charge distribution measured at a distance $x$ from the edge transitions from the previously known CM bulk power law $P(q)\sim |q|^{-5/3}$ for small clusters ($|q|< x^{3/2}$), to a novel power law $P(q)\sim |q|^{-7/3}$ for larger clusters ($|q|>x^{3/2}$). In the 1D Pair Injection Model (PIM), where $+1$ and $-1$ charge monomers are injected simultaneously at adjacent sites, the power law distribution $P(q)\sim |q|^{-2}$ cuts off at $|q|\sim L$ in the steady state for long times, and no large growing condensate is formed. We still observe a distance dependent distribution measured from the largest clusters, or an open boundary, with a bulk power law $P(q)\sim |q|^{-2}$ for small clusters ($|q|< x$), and an edge power law $P(q)\sim |q|^{-3}$ for larger clusters ($|q >x$).
2611.31325.title: Condensates and Edge Effects in the Generalised Takayasu Model

2611.31964.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws.
